This book is not a continuation of that story but a collection of short pieces set in the same countryside, with the Blythes seen mostly from outside, as the neighbours see and talk about them.

The first part is set in the years before the First World War. It gathers short stories of Glen St. Mary and the Four Winds district, each complete in itself, about courtships long delayed, family quarrels, mistaken judgements, secrets kept for years, and the small tyrannies of respectable households. Between them come poems attributed to Anne Blythe and to her son Walter, and short scenes at Ingleside in which the family reads those poems aloud and comments on them and on the neighbours. The Blythes are not the subject of the stories; they are the fixed point the district measures itself against, quoted approvingly by some characters and resented by others, and the effect is to show the familiar world of the earlier books from the outside. The register is drier and more ironic than the novels, and unhappy situations are more often left unrepaired.

The second part is set after the war. The Blythe household is older and Walter is dead, and the linking scenes at Ingleside are quieter, with his verses read aloud among the family and his absence present in the talk. The stories continue as before, drawn from the private lives of the district: marriages made and broken, old grudges, deceptions discovered too late, and lives narrowed by pride or by respectability, with several endings that offer no consolation at all. The Blythes remain at the margins, quoted and discussed by people who mostly know them only by reputation. The collection ends there, without a plot to conclude, leaving Glen St. Mary as it stands after the war and closing the sequence that began with an orphan child arriving at Green Gables.

characters.description: An elderly resident of St Mary Mead whose close study of ordinary behaviour gives her an unusual ability to recognize deception. Dolly Bantry asks for her help when a stranger's body appears at Gossington Hall.
characters.name: Miss Jane Marple

characters.description: Miss Marple's energetic friend and the mistress of Gossington Hall. Faced with a dead stranger in her library, she is determined to learn the truth and protect her husband from malicious gossip.
characters.name: Dolly Bantry

characters.description: Dolly's retired military husband. He is bewildered and deeply embarrassed when a young woman's body is discovered in his library, despite having no apparent connection to her.
characters.name: Colonel Arthur Bantry

characters.description: A young dance hostess at the Majestic Hotel whose disappearance becomes linked to the body at Gossington Hall. Her prospects had recently improved through the interest of a wealthy hotel guest.
characters.name: Ruby Keene

characters.description: Ruby Keene's older cousin and fellow dancer at the Majestic. Practical and protective, she had brought Ruby into the hotel's entertainment staff and reports her missing.
characters.name: Josie Turner

characters.description: A wealthy invalid staying at the Majestic Hotel. After losing his children in an accident, he lives with their surviving spouses and has taken a strong paternal interest in Ruby.
characters.name: Conway Jefferson

characters.description: Conway Jefferson's son-in-law, widowed by the accident that killed Jefferson's children. Sociable and financially pressed, he remains part of Jefferson's household at the hotel.
characters.name: Mark Gaskell

characters.description: Conway Jefferson's widowed daughter-in-law and the mother of Peter Carmody. Quietly capable, she is considering a future beyond continued dependence on her father-in-law.
characters.name: Adelaide Jefferson

characters.description: Adelaide's observant young son and Conway Jefferson's grandson. He collects facts about crime with more enthusiasm than tact.
characters.name: Peter Carmody

characters.description: A flamboyant young man connected with the film industry who lives near Gossington Hall. His late-night movements and acquaintance with dancers draw early police attention.
characters.name: Basil Blake

characters.description: A teenage Girl Guide who disappears after attending an evening meeting. Her case initially seems separate from the death at Gossington Hall.
characters.name: Pamela Reeves

characters.description: The chief constable overseeing the investigation. He knows the Bantrys personally and works with Inspector Slack while remaining open to Miss Marple's observations.
characters.name: Colonel Melchett

recaps.ending: Miss Marple proves that the body in the Bantrys' library was Pamela Reeves, disguised to resemble Ruby Keene, while the burned body in George Bartlett's car was Ruby. Josie Turner and Mark Gaskell arranged the substitution to produce a false timeline and protect their alibis. Conway Jefferson intended to adopt Ruby and leave her a large settlement, reducing the inheritance expected by Mark and Josie. Josie killed both girls and Mark helped execute the plan. Miss Marple uses a false claim about overlooked evidence to provoke Josie into trying to silence Jefferson, allowing the police to catch her. Mark is also arrested. The Bantrys are cleared of scandal, and Jefferson is left to rebuild his family life without the conspirators who exploited him.
recaps.in_short: A young blonde woman is found dead in the Bantrys' library, although nobody in the household knows her. She is identified as hotel dancer Ruby Keene, whose growing closeness to wealthy Conway Jefferson threatened the expectations of his dependent family. A second missing girl, Pamela Reeves, is apparently found burned in a car, but Miss Marple notices that the two deaths have been arranged around a swapped identity. The library body is Pamela disguised as Ruby; the burned victim is the real Ruby. Josie Turner murdered both young women, and Mark Gaskell helped her construct the alibis and false chronology, because Jefferson planned to adopt Ruby and give her money they expected to inherit. Miss Marple lays a trap, Josie and Mark are arrested, and the Bantrys are publicly cleared.

recaps.text: Dolly Bantry wakes to extraordinary news: the body of an unknown young woman in evening dress has been found in the library at Gossington Hall. Neither she nor Colonel Bantry recognizes the victim. Dolly summons Miss Marple before village gossip can settle on her husband. The police trace the dead woman to Ruby Keene, a dance hostess missing from the Majestic Hotel. Basil Blake, a film worker living nearby, appears to offer a possible link between the glamorous stranger and the quiet country house, but the placement of the body still makes little sense.

At the Majestic, Miss Marple and the investigators learn that Ruby had attracted the affectionate attention of the wealthy invalid Conway Jefferson. He had lost his children in an accident and now supports their widowed spouses, Mark Gaskell and Adelaide Jefferson, along with Adelaide's son Peter. Jefferson's intention to make a substantial provision for Ruby gives several people a financial reason to resent her. Ruby's cousin Josie Turner describes the girl's last evening, while hotel guest George Bartlett cannot account cleanly for his car. The inquiry also reaches Basil Blake, but his concealment of the body does not explain the killing itself. Meanwhile, a schoolgirl named Pamela Reeves is reported missing.

A burned body is discovered in Bartlett's abandoned car and is believed to be Pamela Reeves, apparently connecting her disappearance to Ruby's murder. Miss Marple questions the identification process and studies small discrepancies in the dead dancer's appearance, clothing, and habits. Pamela's movements suggest that she was lured by the promise of a screen test or performance opportunity. The evidence now points toward a deliberate attempt to make two victims exchange places in the official chronology. Jefferson's planned financial gift remains the central motive, while the apparent times of death give the people closest to him carefully constructed alibis.

Miss Marple establishes that Pamela Reeves, dressed and made up to resemble Ruby Keene, was the body left in the Bantrys' library. The burned body in the car was Ruby herself, killed later. Josie Turner murdered both girls, and Mark Gaskell assisted with the substitution and disposal. They acted because Conway Jefferson planned to adopt Ruby and settle money on her, cutting into what they expected from him. The swapped identities created a misleading sequence of deaths and supported their alibis. Miss Marple falsely suggests that decisive evidence survived, prompting Josie to make an incriminating attempt to silence Jefferson. Josie and Mark are arrested, Basil Blake is cleared of murder, and the truth removes the cloud of suspicion over Colonel Bantry.

characters.description: A young German girl sent to live with foster parents in a small town near Munich at the start of the Second World War, after her brother's death and the loss of her mother. Grieving and unable to read at first, she steals her first book at her brother's graveside and grows into a passionate reader, finding refuge from a frightening world in words and stories.
characters.name: Liesel Meminger

characters.description: Liesel's foster father, a gentle, quiet housepainter who plays the accordion. Patient and deeply kind, he wins the frightened girl's trust, sits with her through her nightmares, and teaches her to read in the small hours of the night.
characters.name: Hans Hubermann

characters.description: Liesel's foster mother, a stout, sharp-tongued woman who takes in washing to help the household scrape by. Gruff and quick to scold, she hides a fierce loyalty and love for her family beneath a coarse and blustering manner.
characters.name: Rosa Hubermann

characters.description: The lemon-haired boy next door who becomes Liesel's best friend and constant companion. Bold, loyal, and mischievous, he idolizes the athlete Jesse Owens and is forever hoping, in vain, that Liesel will give him a kiss.
characters.name: Rudy Steiner

characters.description: A young Jewish man whom the Hubermanns shelter from the Nazis, hiding him in their home at enormous risk. A fighter by temperament and haunted by what is happening to his people, he forms a deep bond with Liesel through their shared love of words and the stories he writes for her.
characters.name: Max Vandenburg

characters.description: The narrator of the story, a weary, watchful personification of death who gathers up the souls of the dying throughout the war. Curious about human nature and unexpectedly compassionate, Death is haunted and fascinated by the girl whose story it tells.
characters.name: Death

characters.description: The grieving, withdrawn wife of the town's mayor, who lost a son years earlier. She quietly notices Liesel's hunger for books and opens her personal library to the girl, offering a wordless kindness across the gulf between their stations.
characters.name: Ilsa Hermann

recaps.ending: The war closes in on Himmel Street with devastating finality. After the Hubermanns are forced to send Max away for the household's safety, and after Liesel glimpses him again among a column of prisoners driven through the town, the street is destroyed in a nighttime bombing raid that catches everyone asleep. Liesel alone survives, because she had been down in the basement writing the story of her own life, and she emerges to find her foster father Hans, her foster mother Rosa, and her beloved friend Rudy among the dead, along with nearly all their neighbors. Death, the narrator, gathers the souls and keeps the book Liesel dropped in the rubble. Liesel is taken in and grows up, and Max survives the concentration camps; the two are reunited after the war. She goes on to live a long life far from Germany, marrying and raising a family, and dies as an old woman many years later. Death, who has carried her story all this time, finally comes for her and returns the book she wrote, reflecting on how a single human life, amid so much horror, could contain such love and such words.
recaps.in_short: Narrated by Death, the story follows Liesel Meminger, a German girl sent in 1939 to foster parents on Himmel Street in a small town near Munich after her brother dies and her mother disappears. Her kind foster father, Hans Hubermann, teaches her to read, and books become her comfort as Nazi Germany goes to war. She befriends the loyal neighbor boy Rudy Steiner and steals books wherever she can, even snatching one from a Nazi book burning. When the Hubermanns hide a young Jewish man, Max Vandenburg, in their basement, Liesel forms a deep friendship with him, and the household lives in constant danger. Through air raids, hunger, and the cruelties of the regime, Liesel keeps reading and begins to write her own story. In the end, a bombing destroys Himmel Street and kills nearly everyone Liesel loves while she survives by chance in the basement. Max lives through the camps, and years later they are reunited; Liesel goes on to a long life, her book eventually kept by Death itself.

recaps.text: Narrated by Death, who collects the souls of the dying and is drawn to one particular girl, the story begins in 1939 as young Liesel Meminger is sent to live with foster parents in the small town of Molching, near Munich, in Nazi Germany. On the journey her little brother dies, and at his graveside the illiterate Liesel steals her first book. Her new foster parents are the gentle, accordion-playing housepainter Hans Hubermann, who patiently teaches her to read and comforts her through her nightmares, and his gruff, sharp-tongued wife, Rosa. On Himmel Street she befriends the daring, lemon-haired boy next door, Rudy Steiner. As Adolf Hitler's grip tightens and the country marches toward war, Liesel discovers a hunger for books and words that will shape everything to come, stealing volumes where she can and finding in reading a refuge from a dangerous and darkening world.

characters.description: A Blackguard inductee and the Prism's acknowledged bastard, sixteen years old and newly notorious after the disaster at Ru. He is a polychrome of unusual range, he can live other people's memories through a handful of ancient cards, and he is carrying an artifact that strips drafters of their magic. With his father missing and presumed dead, the only Guile left to deal with him is the grandfather who has spent two books deciding whether he is worth keeping.
characters.name: Kip

characters.description: The man the world knew as the Prism, in fact Dazen Guile wearing his brother's stolen name. He came out of the battle at Ru without a scrap of magic and was pulled from the sea by a pirate. He is now an oar slave with no colours, no rank, no leverage and no proof of who he is, and he is a very long way from the Jaspers.
characters.name: Gavin Guile

characters.description: The real Gavin Guile, sixteen years in a nest of coloured cells beneath the Chromeria, breaking out of one only to find the next. He is the reason his brother's colours have been failing, and he is still working.
characters.name: The prisoner

characters.description: Karris Guile, married and widowed inside a season, a Blackguard whose husband is officially dead and who is not permitted to grieve in public. The White takes her out of the Blackguard and puts her to work as an agent instead, which turns out to be an education in how the Chromeria is really run.
characters.name: Karris

characters.description: The head of House Guile and the Spectrum's Red, who now has a vacant Prism's office, a war going badly, and no rival of his own weight left standing. He works entirely from a dark room and expects the succession to go the way he arranges it.
characters.name: Andross Guile

characters.description: The White, head of the Chromeria's administration and openly dying. She spends what she has left arranging the things that will outlast her, including who succeeds her and who is placed where before Andross Guile can fill every seat himself.
characters.name: The White

characters.description: A Blackguard and a paryl drafter, the only one anyone knows of. Because paryl is invisible and undocumented, she is the one asset the Chromeria has that can go where nothing else can, which is why she is asked to do something no inductee should be asked to do.
characters.name: Teia

characters.description: Commander of the Blackguard, who lost a Prism on his watch and is now protecting an institution that is quietly turning on itself. He holds his people together while the Spectrum argues over what a Blackguard is for.
characters.name: Ironfist

characters.description: The best of Kip's squad and its commander in everything but name: fast, principled and stubbornly loyal, holding the group together as the reasons to stay at the Chromeria run out.
characters.name: Cruxer

characters.description: A pirate captain and cannoneer of genuine and unstable genius, who has a rower on his ship he suspects is worth more than the ship. His decisions are made by whim, superstition and whatever will make the better story about Gunner.
characters.name: Gunner

characters.description: Aliviana Danavis, now well past anything the Chromeria taught her, working for the rebellion on the banes: the vast floating bodies of luxin that the old accounts say are where gods are made. She has stopped arguing with herself about which side she is on.
characters.name: Aliviana Danavis

characters.description: The burned man leading the rebellion, whose armies now hold Tyrea and most of Atash and whose declared aim is the end of the Chromeria and of the Freeing. His interest in the banes suggests his ambitions run past politics.
characters.name: The Color Prince

characters.description: A young noblewoman of the Malargos family of Ruthgar, beautiful, well trained in the uses of both, and sent to attach herself to Kip because her house wants something from the Guiles. She is far better at politics than Kip is, and rather less cynical than her instructions require.
characters.name: Tisis Malargos

characters.description: An assassin of the Order of the Broken Eye, the society the Chromeria has insisted for centuries was destroyed. He is a paryl drafter, he can move unseen, he is meticulous, chatty and entirely without limits, and he collects teeth.
characters.name: Murder Sharp

characters.description: A young red drafter brought to the Chromeria as a claimant to the empty Prism's office, presented with paperwork the Spectrum finds hard to argue with. Charming in public and hollow underneath, he was last seen doing the rebellion's work.
characters.name: Zymun

recaps.ending: Gavin gets back to the Jaspers under his own power and is beaten there by his father. Andross has him blinded and put in the deepest of the coloured cells beneath the Chromeria: the prison Gavin built himself, for the brother he stole a name from. No one outside that room knows he is alive. The Order of the Broken Eye is exposed as a live organisation with people inside the Chromeria's own walls, and Teia is left inside it, cut off from anyone who can vouch for her and carrying an invisibility cloak she is not supposed to have. Orea Pullawr dies and Karris is raised to the White, an office she never wanted, at the youngest age anyone can remember, with Andross Guile installed opposite her and Zymun confirmed as Prism-elect. Kip cannot stay: his grandfather has made the Jaspers lethal for him, so he leaves with his squad, marrying Tisis Malargos on the way out because the marriage buys them an army's worth of allies in Ruthgar and the Blood Forest. The rebellion, unopposed, holds most of two satrapies. The Seven Satrapies end the book with a boy king for a Prism, a young widow for a White, an old man holding the real power, and their actual Prism blind in a hole under their feet.
recaps.in_short: The Prism is presumed dead at Ru, and the Chromeria fills the hole with whoever is nearest: Andross Guile takes control of the succession and produces Zymun, a charming psychopath who turns out to be the son Karris bore and lost before the war. The dying White sends Teia into the Order of the Broken Eye, the assassins' society the Chromeria claims to have wiped out, where she is trained by the killer Murder Sharp and given a cloak that makes her invisible. Kip fights his grandfather across a card table and a city, survives repeated attempts on his life, and is pushed into an alliance-marriage with Tisis Malargos. Gavin, an oar slave with no magic, works his way off Gunner's ship and back to the Jaspers, where his father takes him, blinds him, and locks him in the deepest of the cells he once built for his brother. Orea Pullawr dies and Karris is made the White. Kip and his squad flee the Jaspers for the Blood Forest, and the rebellion keeps everything it has taken.

recaps.text: Previously: drafters in the Seven Satrapies turn light into luxin and shorten their lives doing it, and are killed by the Prism in a rite called the Freeing when their power runs out. The man the world calls Gavin Guile is really his brother Dazen, who won the False Prism's War sixteen years ago, took the dead-seeming Gavin's name and office, and has kept the real Gavin alive ever since in a set of nested coloured cells below the Chromeria. Every cell the prisoner breaks costs the false Prism that colour. Kip, a Tyrean boy claimed as Gavin's bastard, came to the Chromeria carrying a jewelled dagger that turned out to be an ancient artifact capable of stripping a drafter's magic. He got through Blackguard training and made a squad of friends there, including Teia, a slave who drafts the invisible colour paryl. Liv Danavis defected to the Color Prince, the burned man leading a rebellion that has taken Tyrea and marched into Atash. Gavin buried his own mother at the Freeing, married Karris White Oak against his father's wishes, then destroyed the rebellion's bane at Ru at the cost of every colour he had. Powerless and unrecognised, he was fished out of the sea by the pirate Gunner. The satrapies were told their Prism was dead.

Gavin is an oar slave. He has no magic, no name he can use, and no way of proving anything to anyone, so he survives by being useful to Gunner, who is unpredictable and much cleverer than he looks. On the Jaspers the Prism is mourned, the war is going badly, and the vacancy at the top of the Chromeria is the only thing the Spectrum can concentrate on. Andross Guile begins arranging the succession. Karris, widowed within weeks of her wedding, is taken out of the Blackguard by the White and put to work as her agent, which is a promotion disguised as a demotion. Kip is left at the Chromeria as the least defended Guile alive, and the attempts on him start almost at once.

Orea Pullawr, the White, is dying and knows roughly how long she has. She spends it placing people. Teia is the piece she cannot replace: paryl is invisible, undocumented and exactly what the Chromeria's enemies use, so the White asks her to go into the Order of the Broken Eye as a spy, with Karris as her only handler and no way to prove her loyalty if she is caught by either side. Kip, meanwhile, keeps being drawn back to the ancient cards, which let a viewer live the memories of the dead, and to what they show about his own family's history. Andross wants the cards, the knife, and Kip out of the way, in roughly that order.

Teia is taken in by the Order and trained by Murder Sharp, a paryl drafter and assassin who is patient, talkative and entirely unhinged, and who teaches her things the Chromeria refuses to admit are possible. The Order proves to be old, wealthy and embedded, with members inside the Chromeria itself. Kip survives another attempt on his life and is approached by Tisis Malargos, a Ruthgari noblewoman whose family has its own claim on the Guiles and who has been sent to make herself useful to him. Karris runs Teia, works the White's networks, and starts to see the shape of the thing her mother-in-law's family has been doing for decades. Gavin, still at sea, begins to work out how to get off the ship.

Andross produces a claimant for the Prism's office: Zymun, a young red drafter with documents the Spectrum cannot easily dismiss. Zymun is the same charming, empty young man who was travelling with the rebellion, and nothing about his arrival is an accident. Kip finally beats his grandfather across the card table, and discovers that Andross does not consider a loss binding. Teia earns her place in the Order the only way it can be earned, and is given a shimmercloak, a garment that makes its wearer effectively invisible, of which the Order holds the last few in the world. Liv, out with the rebellion, is working on the banes: the enormous floating islands of luxin that the old accounts say are where the old gods are seeded and grown.

Zymun's parentage comes out: he is the child Karris bore before the war and was told she would never see, taken from her and raised elsewhere by arrangement of the family that now wants him crowned. Karris has to sit opposite the son she lost and recognise what he is. Teia goes deeper into the Order and finds that its ambitions are not simply murder for hire; it wants the Chromeria's whole structure gone, and it has been waiting a very long time. Gavin gets himself off Gunner's ship and starts the long journey back toward the Jaspers, blind to how much has changed. Kip's position at the Chromeria becomes untenable, and Tisis, whatever her instructions were, stops following them exactly.

Zymun is confirmed as Prism-elect, which puts the succession in Andross Guile's hand and a murderer in the Chromeria's highest office. The White is failing fast and finishes arranging what she can. The Order sets its plan for Sun Day, the festival that gathers every important person in the satrapies into the same few streets, and Teia has to decide how much she can let happen in order to stay inside it. Kip is formally moved against by his grandfather and finds that being a Guile protects him from nothing. His squad closes around him.

Gavin comes back to the Jaspers under his own power, without magic, without allies, and without anyone expecting him. Karris is being groomed for an office she does not want. Andross is one ceremony away from owning the Chromeria outright. The Order's people are in position across Big Jasper. Teia, cloaked and alone, is in the middle of it with no way to signal anyone, and the assassins she has been living with are about to do the thing she was sent in to prevent.

Sun Day comes apart. The Order strikes in the open, the Blackguard fights in the streets, and the ceremony that was meant to install a new Prism becomes a battle. Teia moves against Murder Sharp and the Order's plan from inside it, at the price of any hope of coming back out clean. Kip and his squad fight through the city. Gavin reaches the Chromeria in the middle of the chaos and gets far enough to confront his father, who has been ready for him longer than he has been alive.

Andross wins. He has Gavin blinded and shut in the deepest of the coloured cells beneath the Chromeria, the prison Gavin built for the brother whose name he took, and no one else is told he is alive. Orea Pullawr dies, and her arrangements hold: Karris is raised to the White, the youngest in memory, opposite Andross Guile and above a Prism-elect who is her own lost son. Teia is left inside the Order, unable to prove what she is to anyone, holding a shimmercloak she was never meant to keep. Kip cannot survive another week on the Jaspers, so he leaves with his squad, and marries Tisis Malargos on the way out because that marriage is worth allies, money and a place to stand in Ruthgar and the Blood Forest. The rebellion, unopposed all season, holds two satrapies and is still growing its banes. The Seven Satrapies close the book with a boy for a Prism, a widow for a White, an old man holding everything that matters, and the real Prism blind in a hole under the tower.

characters.description: The second Hawthorne brother, precise, self-contained, and used to being the one who fixes things without being asked. He carries what happened to his biological father and the family's decision to bury it, and he goes to Phoenix to make sure the family that man left behind is provided for, intending never to tell them who he is.
characters.name: Grayson Hawthorne

characters.description: The third Hawthorne brother, addicted to risk and to being tested, and the one member of the family who has never met his own father. When that father turns up wanting his help, Jameson takes the invitation for the same reason he takes every invitation: to find out whether he can win.
characters.name: Jameson Winchester Hawthorne

characters.description: The heir to the Hawthorne fortune, now in control of it and giving it away on her own terms, and Jameson's partner in whatever he decides to gamble on next.
characters.name: Avery Kylie Grambs

characters.description: The oldest Hawthorne brother, the family's steadying influence, uninterested in the money and attached to Libby.
characters.name: Nash Hawthorne

characters.description: Avery's older half-sister, who has come a long way from a diner job and a bad boyfriend and is now part of the Hawthorne household in her own right.
characters.name: Libby Grambs

characters.description: The youngest Hawthorne brother, inventor and enthusiast, off pursuing projects of his own while his brothers are abroad and in Arizona.
characters.name: Alexander Hawthorne

characters.description: One of Sheffield Grayson's twin daughters: disciplined, competitive, and impossible to read, holding her family together by refusing to let any strain show. She gives away nothing about her father, including how much she knows.
characters.name: Savannah Grayson

characters.description: Savannah's twin, relentlessly cheerful and curious about everything, with a habit of talking her way into places she should not be. Once she starts pulling at the question of what happened to her father, she cannot leave it alone.
characters.name: Gigi Grayson

characters.description: Jameson's biological father, an English charmer with expensive habits and a talent for making his own problems sound like someone else's opportunity. He needs something only a private London establishment can grant, and he needs a Hawthorne to win it for him.
characters.name: Ian Johnstone-Jameson

characters.description: Sheffield Grayson's wife, left with two teenage daughters, a husband who vanished without explanation, and an estate she cannot get at. She is holding a household together on appearances and dwindling resources.
characters.name: Acacia Grayson

characters.description: The factotum of the Devil's Mercy, the young man who runs the club's floor on the proprietor's behalf and enjoys every part of the work. He decides who is tested for entry and how, keeps the house's secrets, and plays as hard as anyone at its tables.
characters.name: Rohan

characters.description: The unseen head of the Devil's Mercy, whose identity is among the club's most closely kept secrets and whose word is its only law. What the house grants, it grants at the proprietor's discretion.
characters.name: The Proprietor

recaps.ending: Grayson stops hiding: he tells Savannah and Gigi who he is and what he knows about their father, and instead of losing them he ends the book with two sisters, their mother's household secured, and the scheme that was stripping the Grayson estate broken. The twins are now part of the Hawthorne orbit rather than a secret Grayson keeps from it, and Savannah's own long silence about their father is finally out in the open. In London, Jameson wins his way into the Devil's Mercy and wins its game, taking his father's measure in the process and refusing to be the instrument Ian intended; Ian ends the book without the leverage he came for, and Rohan's standing inside the club is transformed by what happens. Jameson and Avery leave London with a much better sense of what the Hawthorne name is worth outside Texas. The brothers come home to a family larger than the one they started the book with, and Avery's plan to turn the fortune into a game that ordinary people can enter moves closer to its first running.
recaps.in_short: The fourth book splits between two brothers on separate errands. Grayson goes to Phoenix to quietly look after the family his biological father left behind, a wife and twin daughters who have no idea the man is dead or that Grayson is related to them, and finds their money gone and their affairs being picked over. Savannah keeps her composure and her secrets; Gigi starts investigating her father's disappearance and pulls the whole thing open. Jameson, meanwhile, is approached by Ian Johnstone-Jameson, the English father he has never met, who needs him to win a favor from the Devil's Mercy, a private London club where the stakes are debts and favors rather than money. Jameson has to win his way in through trials set by Rohan, the club's factotum, with Avery beside him and his father's account of what he needs shifting every time it is told. Both brothers end up choosing honesty over the plan they arrived with: Grayson tells the twins the truth and claims them as family, and Jameson wins the club's game and refuses to be used by his father.

recaps.text: Avery Kylie Grambs inherited billions from Tobias Hawthorne, a Texas billionaire she had never met, who cut out his own daughters and his four grandsons: Nash, Grayson, Jameson, and Xander. Across three books she survived several attempts on her life, solved the puzzles the old man left behind, and found his son Toby, who had been presumed dead for twenty years. Grayson's biological father, Sheffield Grayson, was behind the second wave of attacks and died in the confrontation; the Hawthornes concealed it, leaving his wife and twin daughters in Phoenix believing only that he had disappeared. In the third book the family faced Vincent Blake, the patriarch of a rival clan who held Toby captive and knew what had become of Sheffield Grayson. Avery beat Blake on his own ground, freed Toby, turned eighteen, and took full control of the fortune, which she has been deliberately giving away ever since. She and Jameson are together, Nash and Libby are together, and Xander is pursuing his own projects. Grayson has never told the family his father left behind what really happened, and Jameson has never met his own father at all.

The book follows two brothers on separate errands. Grayson travels to Phoenix, where the family Sheffield Grayson left behind, his wife Acacia and their twin daughters Savannah and Gigi, are coping with a vanished man, a frozen estate, and money that has stopped arriving. Grayson does not tell them who he is or what he knows about their father's fate. Jameson, meanwhile, is approached by Ian Johnstone-Jameson, the English father he has never met, who wants his help winning something from the Devil's Mercy, a private London establishment where the currency is favors, secrets, and debts rather than cash.

In Phoenix, Grayson finds two sisters coping in opposite directions. Savannah is disciplined, guarded, and determined to give nothing away, while Gigi is relentlessly curious and has already begun digging into what happened to their father. Keeping his identity to himself gets harder the further into their lives he is drawn. In London, Jameson learns that the Devil's Mercy admits nobody who has not won their way in, and that the terms are set by Rohan, the young factotum who runs the floor for the club's unseen proprietor. Avery comes with him. Ian's account of what he needs, and why he needs a Hawthorne to get it, changes a little every time he tells it.

Gigi's investigation turns up the parts of her father's business she was never meant to see, and the people benefiting from his absence would rather the questions stopped. Grayson has to work out how much protection he can give the twins without explaining who he is, and finds himself acting like a brother rather than a benefactor. In London, Jameson takes on the trials that decide who is admitted to the Devil's Mercy, competing against people who have spent far longer preparing for the chance, and discovers that Rohan plays the club's games as well as any Hawthorne and knows the house's secrets besides.

Both brothers reach the point where the cover story stops working. In Phoenix the scheme around the Grayson estate comes into focus, Savannah reveals how much she has known all along about her father and what he was involved in, and Grayson's own connection to the family becomes impossible to keep from them. In London, Jameson wins his place inside the Devil's Mercy and finds out what his father actually wants the club's favor for, and how far Ian has been prepared to gamble with his son to get it.

Grayson decides that the twins matter more than the version of events he came to Phoenix protecting, and turns Hawthorne resources on the people exploiting their father's absence in order to salvage what is left of the family's position. In London, Jameson plays for the favor the Devil's Mercy grants, against opponents who know the house far better than he does and against his father's plans for the prize. Rohan's own ambitions for the club become clear, and Jameson has to decide whether his father is someone to be won over or simply another player at the table.

Grayson tells Savannah and Gigi who he is and what happened to their father, and rather than losing them he ends the book with two sisters, their mother's household on solid ground, and the scheme against the Grayson estate broken. In London, Jameson wins the game at the Devil's Mercy, takes his father's measure, and refuses to be the instrument Ian wanted, leaving Ian without the leverage he came for; Rohan's position inside the club is transformed by the outcome. Jameson and Avery return with a clearer sense of how far the Hawthorne name reaches beyond Texas, the brothers are reunited with a family larger than the one they began with, and Avery's plan to open the fortune up as a game ordinary players can enter moves toward its first running.

characters.description: The father of the Karamazov brothers, a coarse, buffoonish, and dissolute landowner. Sensual, greedy, and shameless, he has squandered attention on his own pleasures while neglecting his sons, and he delights in provoking and humiliating those around him. His appetites and his quarrels over money and women, especially his rivalry with his eldest son over Grushenka, set much of the story's conflict in motion.
characters.name: Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov

characters.description: The eldest brother, a passionate, impulsive former army officer given to extremes of feeling. Generous and reckless, honorable in his ideals yet undisciplined in his conduct, he is entangled in bitter disputes with his father over an inheritance and over the beautiful Grushenka, while also bound by an engagement to the proud Katerina Ivanovna. His stormy nature keeps him on the edge of scandal.
characters.name: Dmitri Karamazov

characters.description: The middle brother, cold, brilliant, and intellectual. A skeptic and a rationalist, he wrestles openly with questions of God, morality, and human suffering, and cannot reconcile faith with the cruelty he sees in the world. Reserved and proud, he keeps his deepest torments to himself, and his ideas exert a powerful influence on those around him.
characters.name: Ivan Karamazov

characters.description: The youngest brother and the novel's gentle moral center. A kind, guileless young man who has entered the local monastery as a novice under the elder Zosima, he is loved and trusted by nearly everyone. Compassionate and clear-eyed, he moves between his warring family members and the wider community, trying to bring understanding and peace.
characters.name: Alexei Karamazov

characters.description: A sullen, secretive servant in Fyodor Pavlovich's household, employed as a cook, and widely rumored to be Fyodor's illegitimate son by a local woman. Epileptic, resentful, and cunning, he affects servility while nursing private contempt, and he listens closely to the ideas of the educated men around him.
characters.name: Pavel Smerdyakov

characters.description: A proud, alluring young woman with a troubled past and a sharp will. Both Fyodor Pavlovich and his son Dmitri pursue her, and their rivalry over her fuels the family's crisis. Capricious and self-protective, she guards herself against being used, and her feelings and loyalties are not easily read.
characters.name: Agrafena Svetlova

characters.description: Dmitri's proud, strong-willed fiancee, a woman of high social standing bound to him by a debt of gratitude and a sense of duty. Intense and self-dramatizing, she is torn between her attachment to Dmitri and other feelings she struggles to admit, and her pride shapes her every decision.
characters.name: Katerina Ivanovna

characters.description: A revered elder at the local monastery and Alyosha's spiritual mentor. Wise, humble, and deeply loving, he preaches active love, forgiveness, and responsibility for all, and is sought out by pilgrims and troubled souls alike. His teaching and example form the moral counterweight to the Karamazov family's chaos.
characters.name: Elder Zosima

characters.description: A proud, sensitive schoolboy from a poor and humiliated family, fiercely devoted to his disgraced father. Bullied and defensive, he becomes the focus of a group of local boys whom Alyosha befriends and guides.
characters.name: Ilyusha Snegiryov

characters.description: A cynical, ambitious young seminarian who moves in the same circles as the Karamazovs. Clever and self-interested, he cloaks his careerism in progressive talk, and observes the family's troubles with a calculating eye.
characters.name: Mikhail Rakitin

recaps.ending: Fyodor Pavlovich is murdered and robbed, and Dmitri, who had quarreled violently with his father and cannot fully account for that night, is charged with the crime. At his trial, despite the passionate defense mounted on his behalf, the circumstantial case overwhelms him and he is convicted of killing his father and sentenced to penal servitude in Siberia. The real murderer is the servant Smerdyakov, who killed Fyodor after concluding, from Ivan's teaching that in a world without God all things are permitted, that he was licensed to act; he reveals this to Ivan in a series of confrontations and then hangs himself, leaving no confession the court will accept. Ivan, crushed by guilt and haunted by a hallucination of the devil, breaks down into a feverish madness. Katerina Ivanovna and Grushenka are left to their divided loves, and a scheme is set in motion to help Dmitri flee his sentence. The novel closes not on the courtroom but on the funeral of the boy Ilyusha, where Alyosha urges the assembled schoolboys to hold on to their good memories and their love for one another, offering a note of faith and renewal against the family's ruin.
recaps.in_short: The dissolute landowner Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov and his three very different sons - the passionate Dmitri, the intellectual Ivan, and the gentle novice Alyosha - are drawn into bitter conflict over money and over the young woman Grushenka, whom both Fyodor and Dmitri pursue. When Fyodor is found murdered and robbed, suspicion falls on Dmitri, who had publicly threatened his father and was near the house that night, though he insists he is innocent. He is arrested, tried, and convicted of parricide on powerful circumstantial evidence. In truth the killer is the servant Smerdyakov, who acted after absorbing Ivan's argument that without God everything is permitted; Smerdyakov confesses privately to Ivan and then hangs himself, while Ivan, tormented by his share of guilt, collapses into brain fever and delirium. Dmitri is sentenced to hard labor in Siberia, with a plan afoot to help him escape. Alongside the family tragedy runs the story of Alyosha and a group of schoolboys around the dying child Ilyusha, ending on Alyosha's message of love, memory, and hope.

recaps.text: In a Russian provincial town, the coarse and dissolute landowner Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov has three grown sons by two marriages, all of them shaped by his neglect. Dmitri, the eldest, is a hot-blooded, spendthrift former officer locked in a furious dispute with his father over an inheritance and over the beautiful, unpredictable Grushenka, whom both men want. Ivan is a brilliant, brooding skeptic tormented by questions of God and human suffering. Alyosha, the youngest, is a gentle novice at the local monastery under the saintly elder Zosima, and serves as a trusted go-between for his quarreling relatives. Complicating the tangle are Dmitri's proud fiancee Katerina Ivanovna and the sullen, secretive servant Smerdyakov, rumored to be Fyodor's illegitimate son. The premise gathers this volatile family and its rivalries of money, faith, and desire around Fyodor Pavlovich, whose greed and provocations push the household toward catastrophe.

characters.description: The exiled rebel lord who has spent fifteen years in the Mountains of Rain and Night, and who is now openly preparing to invade Araluen. His attempt to murder the kingdom's senior commanders was stopped, but he is patient and thinks in terms of traps rather than pitched battles. He controls his Wargal army directly with his mind, so it fights with no will of its own.
characters.name: Morgarath

characters.description: Morgarath's soldiers: heavy, black-furred, brutish creatures who fight in silence under his mental control and have no independent will of their own. They are strong and tireless but have one weakness that Araluen has exploited before, an instinctive terror of horses.
characters.name: Wargals

characters.description: A Ranger's apprentice at Redmont, a year further into his training and steadier for it. He is a competent shot, hard to see when he does not want to be seen, and still the smallest person in most rooms he enters. His part in the killing of the Kalkara has given him a reputation he is not entirely comfortable with.
characters.name: Will

characters.description: The King's Ranger for Redmont Fief and Will's teacher: grey, terse, and trusted by the King on matters of war. With Morgarath mobilising, his work turns from watching the fief to advising the kingdom's commanders.
characters.name: Halt

characters.description: A Battleschool apprentice at Redmont and Will's friend, already taller and heavier than most of the boys ahead of him and marked out by his instructors as exceptional with a sword. He is straightforward, literal-minded and steady under pressure.
characters.name: Horace Altman

characters.description: Will's Ranger horse: small, shaggy, barrel-chested and much faster and more intelligent than his appearance suggests.
characters.name: Tug

characters.description: Lord of Redmont Fief, now raising and equipping his fighting men for the war everyone expects.
characters.name: Baron Arald

characters.description: Redmont's Battlemaster, responsible for the fief's knights and apprentices and for readying them to march.
characters.name: Sir Rodney

characters.description: Halt's former apprentice and now the Ranger of a southern fief, cheerful, quick and an accomplished swordsman as well as a Ranger. He is given command of a small mission and treats Will and Horace as junior colleagues rather than children.
characters.name: Gilan

characters.description: The King of Araluen, who defeated Morgarath's rebellion fifteen years earlier and is now assembling the fiefs' armies to meet him again. He is capable, direct, and willing to listen to his Rangers.
characters.name: King Duncan

characters.description: A fair-haired Araluen girl found alone in a deserted Celtican village, the only member of her travelling party to escape when it was attacked. She says she is a maid in the service of Princess Cassandra. She is composed, quick-witted, unwilling to be left behind, and noticeably harder to place than a servant should be.
characters.name: Evanlyn

characters.description: A Skandian jarl, captain of a wolfship and leader of a raiding crew hired as mercenaries. Skandians are northern sea raiders who fight for pay and plunder, and Erak is a big, loud, practical man who treats prisoners as property to be sold rather than as enemies to be killed.
characters.name: Erak

recaps.ending: Morgarath's flanking plan collapses. The bridge his slaves built is burned, and the Wargal column that crosses the gorge is met and destroyed rather than falling on the Araluen army's rear. With his trap gone and his army now facing the King's, Morgarath demands that the matter be settled by single combat. Horace, still a Battleschool apprentice, answers the challenge and kills him. Deprived of the mind that drove them, the surviving Wargals stop fighting. The war that has hung over Araluen since the first book is over in an afternoon, and the kingdom has lost the enemy who defined it. The victory is incomplete for the people at its centre. Will and Evanlyn are not there: they were taken at the bridge by Erak's Skandians and are aboard a wolfship bound north for Skandia, where captives are sold or worked as slaves. In the aftermath it emerges that Evanlyn is not a servant at all but Cassandra, King Duncan's daughter and the heir to Araluen, which makes her capture a far graver matter than anyone holding her yet understands. Halt, refused nothing else by the King, sets himself to getting Will back.
recaps.in_short: With Morgarath massing to invade Araluen, King Duncan sends the Ranger Gilan into neighbouring Celtica to call in its promised troops, with Will and Horace as his companions. They find the country emptied: the villages abandoned, the mines silent, and a lone survivor, a girl called Evanlyn who says she serves Princess Cassandra. The Celts have been taken by Morgarath's Wargals and forced to build a bridge across the gorge that has always protected Araluen's flank, so that an army can come in behind the King's. Gilan rides back to warn the army while the other three stay to watch. They set the bridge alight, but Will and Evanlyn are captured by the Skandian mercenaries guarding it and carried off to sea. Horace reaches the army in time; Halt destroys the Wargal column at the gorge, and when Morgarath demands single combat, Horace fights and kills him. The war ends, but Will and Evanlyn are gone, and Evanlyn is revealed to be Princess Cassandra herself.

recaps.text: Previously: Will, an orphan raised as a ward of Castle Redmont in the kingdom of Araluen, was refused a place in Battleschool and instead apprenticed to Halt, the fief's grim and widely feared Ranger. He learned that the Rangers are the King's scouts and intelligence corps rather than the sorcerers common people take them for, and was trained in concealment, tracking, the knife and the longbow, and given a Ranger horse, Tug. Meanwhile the exiled rebel lord Morgarath, beaten fifteen years earlier and confined since to the Mountains of Rain and Night with his Wargal army, tried to murder Araluen's senior commanders ahead of a new war by sending two Kalkara, huge beasts that arrows barely touch. Halt and his former apprentice Gilan hunted the creatures to the ruins of Morgarath's old castle at Gorlan; Halt killed one, and Will destroyed the second with a burning arrow when it had Halt at its mercy. Will also made peace with Horace, a former tormentor now training as a knight, and turned down a belated offer of Battleschool to stay a Ranger's apprentice. The attempt on the commanders told Araluen that Morgarath was preparing to move, and the fiefs began arming.

Araluen mobilises. Morgarath's army is stirring in the mountains, the fiefs are called out, and the King's council has to work out where the blow will fall, since the only ways down out of the Mountains of Rain and Night are narrow and defensible. Part of the plan depends on Celtica, Araluen's small mining neighbour, which owes a contingent of troops by treaty and has not sent word. Gilan is given the job of riding into Celtica to collect them, and takes Will and Horace with him, partly as messengers and partly because the two apprentices are useful. Halt stays with the army. The three of them cross the border in good spirits, expecting a straightforward diplomatic errand.

Celtica is empty. Village after village stands abandoned with meals half eaten and doors open, the mines are silent, and there is no sign of the army the Araluens came to fetch. In the ruins of one settlement they find a single survivor, an Araluen girl called Evanlyn, who says she is a maid to Princess Cassandra and the only member of her party left alive after it was attacked. From her and from the tracks around them, the three work out that Morgarath's Wargals have swept through the country and driven the Celts off in a body rather than killing them, which means he wants them for something. Gilan decides to follow, and Evanlyn, who has nowhere else to go, comes with them.

The trail leads to the gorge that has always protected the eastern flank of Araluen's defences, and to the answer. Morgarath has worked the captured Celts to death building a bridge across it, so that a Wargal force can cross unseen, come out behind the King's army while it faces the mountain passes, and destroy it between two forces. Gilan grasps at once that the army must be warned or it will be annihilated, and rides for Araluen at his best speed. He leaves Will, Horace and Evanlyn behind to keep watch on the bridge and report what happens there, with orders to avoid contact.

The three watch the crossing and find the work almost finished, with the bridge guarded not only by Wargals but by a hired Skandian crew, northern sea raiders taken on as mercenaries. Waiting for the army to arrive would be too late: once Morgarath's column is across, warning alone will not stop it. Will concludes that the bridge itself has to be destroyed, and the three of them plan how to reach it, get fire into the timbers, and get out again, with Horace's sword the only real protection they have if it goes wrong.

The plan works and then falls apart. The bridge is fired and the crossing ruined, but the noise and flame bring Wargals and Skandians down on them. Horace holds the approach with his sword long enough for the fire to take, killing several Wargals in the process, and is driven off into the country beyond, from where he makes for the Araluen army. Will and Evanlyn are cut off and taken alive by Erak, the Skandian jarl commanding the mercenaries, who values prisoners as property. They are carried away to his wolfship, and Evanlyn keeps up her story of being a servant, since a captured Araluen maid is worth ransom or a slave market, and nothing worse.

Horace reaches the King's army on the Plains of Uthal and reports what the three of them found and did, which is how Halt learns that his apprentice has been taken. The Araluen commanders now know both halves of Morgarath's plan, and Halt takes a force to the gorge to deal with the flanking column as it comes out of the broken crossing. The Wargals are met by horsemen, which they fear instinctively, and the column that was meant to fall on the King's rear is destroyed instead. On the plain, the two main armies form up facing each other, with Morgarath's advantage of surprise gone and his own line now the one in trouble.

With his trap sprung and useless, Morgarath demands that the war be decided by single combat rather than by a battle he is losing. Horace, an apprentice and not yet a knight, takes up the challenge and kills him. The Wargals, who fought only because Morgarath's mind drove them, stop where they stand once he is dead, and the war is over. In the aftermath the King's household learns that the girl who was taken at the bridge is not a maid at all: Evanlyn is Cassandra, King Duncan's daughter and the heir to Araluen, travelling under another name. She and Will are aboard Erak's wolfship, heading north to Skandia, where prisoners are slaves. Halt, having helped win the kingdom's war, turns immediately to the problem of getting Will back.

characters.description: One-handed, permanently anchored to Kitay, and back in the province she was born in, Rin intends to raise Nikan's poorest people into an army and take the country from both the Empire and the Dragon Republic that discarded her. Her fire is under control for the first time in her life; very little else about her is. The southerners who follow her treat her less as a general than as a figure out of their own religion, and she does not discourage it.
characters.name: Rin

characters.description: Rin's anchor and chief strategist, bound to her permanently: he feels what she feels, steadies her mind when the Phoenix has hold of it, and will die if she does. He runs the army's supply and planning and is the only person willing to argue with her about what she does with it.
characters.name: Chen Kitay

characters.description: A Sinegard classmate and survivor of Golyn Niis, now one of Rin's officers and her best marksman. Blunt, impatient and without illusions about anyone she serves with.
characters.name: Sring Venka

characters.description: A Cike veteran who fights with a nine-pointed rake and channels a boar god, and one of the last of the unit still standing.
characters.name: Baji

characters.description: An enormous Cike soldier who channels a monkey god, still fighting to keep it from taking him over for good.
characters.name: Suni

characters.description: The Cike's explosives-maker, the youngest of them, who has kept the unit supplied with fire powder through two wars.
characters.name: Ramsa

characters.description: The deposed empress of Nikan, travelling with Rin as something between prisoner, advisor and hostage. She is a shaman whose god works on perception, she is a great deal older than she appears, and she is the only living person who can explain how the Nikara Empire was actually made and by whom.
characters.name: Su Daji

characters.description: One of the warlords directing the Southern Coalition, the alliance of southern militias that has been fighting the stranded Mugenese occupation without help from the Empire or the Republic. He is willing to use Rin's reputation and unwilling to hand her his army.
characters.name: Gurubai

characters.description: A southern militia commander who has fought the Mugenese occupation with ambushes and local knowledge, and who speaks for the peasant recruits who make up most of the Coalition's strength. Charismatic, plain-spoken and enormously popular with the rank and file, he becomes Rin's closest ally among the southern leadership.
characters.name: Yang Souji

characters.description: Rin's younger foster brother from Tikany, a small child when she left for Sinegard and nearly grown by the time she comes back to a town the war has emptied.
characters.name: Kesegi

characters.description: Rin's rival since Sinegard, now the Dragon Republic's commander in the field and the Hesperians' working partner in Nikan. He is a shaman himself, bound since childhood to a river dragon, and the only person in the country able to meet Rin's fire with anything comparable.
characters.name: Yin Nezha

characters.description: Warlord of the Dragon Province, Nezha's father and head of the Dragon Republic, governing the greater part of Nikan in partnership with the Hesperians who recognised his state and armed it.
characters.name: Yin Vaisra

characters.description: The Hesperian missionary and natural scientist who studied Rin at Arlong and regards shamans as diseased rather than divine. Her order's assessment of Nikan determines how much of the country the Hesperians intend to govern themselves.
characters.name: Sister Petra Ignatius

characters.description: Rin's vanished master from Sinegard, found sealed inside the stone of the Chuluu Korikh: far older than any ordinary man, badly damaged, and lucid only in stretches. The gardener who taught her meditation and refused to fight in her war was one of the three shamans who founded the Nikara Empire.
characters.name: Jiang Ziya

characters.description: The Dragon Emperor: the third of the shamans who drove the Federation out two generations ago and built the Nikara Empire, sealed inside the Chuluu Korikh for decades. Commanding, magnetic and entirely without restraint, he intends to have his country back on his own terms.
characters.name: Yin Riga

recaps.ending: Rin ends the war on the winning side of it. Riga is dead, the Trifecta is finished, the Dragon Republic's armies are broken, and the southern army she raised has effectively taken Nikan. What she does not have is any reason to stop. Her plans run past the Hesperian foothold to the provinces that opposed her, and she is entirely capable of carrying them out. Kitay, bound to her as her anchor and so unable to be absent from any decision she makes, concludes that she will never stop and that nothing outside her can stop her; Nezha, who has fought her since they were schoolchildren, reaches the same conclusion from the other side. The two act together against her. When Rin understands what they have done, she agrees with the reasoning: she chooses her own death rather than be stopped by anyone else, and dies by the fire she spent the whole war learning to command. Nezha is left to govern what remains - a country invaded twice and burned repeatedly, its population devastated, its independence conditional on foreigners it can no longer expel. The uprising Rin led destroyed the old order and cost her her life, and the book closes on that cost stated plainly rather than settled.
recaps.in_short: Maimed and cast out, Rin returns to Nikan's south and turns its militias into an army, clearing the stranded Mugenese occupation and then marching north against the Dragon Republic, which now governs the country in partnership with the Hesperians and which Nezha commands in the field. Betrayed by the southern commander whose peasant regiments carried her, Rin is driven back and gambles on the Chuluu Korikh, where she finds her old master Jiang and the truth about him: Jiang, the deposed empress Daji and the Dragon Emperor Yin Riga are the Trifecta, the three shamans who made the Empire. Rin frees Riga as a weapon and he proves ungovernable; he is killed, and the Trifecta ends with him. Rin then breaks the Republic in the field, but by then she cannot stop, and means to burn everything that will not submit. Kitay, bound to her, and Nezha, who has fought her the whole war, conclude that she has to be stopped; Rin reaches the same conclusion herself and chooses to die, leaving Nezha the ruined country.

recaps.text: Previously: Rin, a war orphan from Nikan's south, won a place at the Sinegard military academy, was apprenticed to the master of Lore, and learned that the old gods are real and can be reached by shamans at the cost of their sanity. Commissioned into the Cike during the Federation's invasion, she served under Altan Trengsin, the last Speerly, through the fall of Khurdalain and the massacre of Golyn Niis. After Altan died freeing her from a Federation research station on Speer, and after she learned that Empress Su Daji had sold Speer to the Federation to end the previous war, Rin called the Phoenix and destroyed the Federation's home islands and their entire population. A year later her attempt to kill Daji failed and cost her access to her god. Recruited by Warlord Yin Vaisra, she fought for his Hesperian-backed Dragon Republic; the campaign was broken at the Red Cliffs by the loosed wind shaman Feylen. Bound at last to an anchor - Kitay, whose life is now tied to hers - she recovered her fire and won the battle of Arlong, and was betrayed immediately: the Hesperians' price for recognising the Republic was Rin herself. She escaped maimed, losing her left hand, taking Kitay, Venka, the last of the Cike and the captive Daji with her, and went south to raise an army from the people both sides had always spent.

Rin reaches the south with Kitay, Venka, the last of the Cike and the deposed empress Daji, and finds the region occupied. Federation soldiers stranded in Nikan when their homeland was destroyed have entrenched themselves across the southern countryside, and the Southern Coalition - an alliance of local militias under warlords the Empire never armed - has been fighting them alone and without supply. Rin offers the Coalition the one thing it lacks: a shaman. In Tikany, the town she grew up in, she finds the household that raised her and a place hollowed out by occupation and by the war she helped end. The southerners, told for generations that they are worth nothing, take to her as something out of their own stories, which is more useful to her than the warlords' cooperation and considerably harder to control.

Rin turns the Coalition's militias into an army and takes over its direction, with Kitay running supply and Souji delivering the peasant recruits who make up its strength. The Mugenese occupation of the south is broken; Rin's methods are total and she does not take prisoners. With the south cleared she turns north against the Dragon Republic, which now governs most of Nikan from Arlong in partnership with the Hesperians, whose ships, guns and airships sit in Nikara harbours. Nezha commands the Republic's armies in the field. The war between them is fought over the same river provinces already ruined twice, and Rin's advantage - a shaman who can burn an army in an afternoon - is answered by a Republic with a shaman of its own and a foreign ally with better machines.

The northern campaign becomes a contest Rin can win in the field and cannot finish. The Republic gives ground, the Hesperians commit more openly, and their airships make her fire less decisive than it was. Daji, travelling with the army, begins trading what she knows for her usefulness: the Empire was not inherited but made, by three shamans who drove the Federation out two generations ago and then divided the country between them, and the empress Rin has spent years hating is only one of the three. What became of the other two, and what Rin's own master had to do with them, is the price Daji sets on her cooperation. Meanwhile the army grows past Rin's ability to feed it, the countryside she is liberating is starving, and Kitay's figures say she is losing the war she appears to be winning.

Rin's position collapses from the inside. Souji, whose peasant regiments are the bulk of her strength, has been dealing with the Republic behind her, and the betrayal costs her a battle, most of an army, and several of the people who have followed her since the Cike. Nezha's forces and the Hesperians take the initiative, and Rin is driven back with a fraction of what she commanded. What is left of her campaign depends on finding power the Republic cannot match, and the only candidates are the shamans still sealed alive inside the Chuluu Korikh - the mountain that produced Feylen the last time anyone opened it. Daji, it becomes clear, has been steering her toward exactly that from the day they left Arlong.

Rin, Kitay and Daji reach the Chuluu Korikh and open it. Inside is Jiang, Rin's master from Sinegard, sealed in the stone for years and barely coherent, and with him the truth about who he is. Jiang, Daji and a third shaman, Yin Riga, are the Trifecta: the three who drove the Federation out two generations ago and built the Nikara Empire on the strength of it. Riga ruled it as the Dragon Emperor, Daji held the throne after him, and Jiang sealed himself away, so that the eccentric gardener Rin knew at Sinegard was a man who had deliberately unmade his own memory. Riga is inside the mountain too, sealed there by Jiang, and both of the others want him back. Rin, needing a weapon the Republic cannot answer, agrees to release him.

Freeing Riga is a catastrophe. The Dragon Emperor is exactly what the histories describe - overwhelming, magnetic and without any limit at all - and he intends to take the country back and use everyone in it, Rin included, as material. Daji cannot refuse him and Jiang can barely resist him. Riga's return threatens the Republic as much as it threatens Rin, and Rin and Nezha end up briefly on the same side against him. Riga is killed and the Trifecta ends with him, at a cost that leaves the survivors of the three broken. Rin comes out of it with her god, her army and no living authority over her whatsoever. The war with the Republic resumes at once, and the Hesperians, having watched what Nikara shamans do to one another, have concluded that the country must be administered rather than allied with.

Rin wins her war and cannot stop fighting it. With Riga gone she breaks the Republic's armies in the field and comes within reach of ruling what is left of Nikan - and by then her intentions have run past the war itself, to the Hesperian foothold, to the provinces that resisted her, and to anything else that will not submit. Kitay, who as her anchor feels every decision she makes, concludes that she will not stop and that nobody outside her can make her; Nezha reaches the same conclusion from the other side, and the two of them act together. Confronted with what they have done and with what remains of the country she fought for, Rin agrees with them. She chooses her own death, and dies by the fire she spent the whole war learning to command. Nezha is left to hold together a country stripped by two invasions and a civil war, under the shadow of a foreign power it cannot expel, and the south's revolution ends with the woman who led it dead by her own decision.

characters.description: Lord of Bebbanburg in name only, now in his thirties: Alfred's greatest warrior and the military governor who holds Lundene for Wessex, though he remains a pagan the pious court distrusts. Married to the Danish Gisela and still dreaming of the northern fortress his uncle stole, he fights Wessex's wars while resenting the oath that keeps him from his own. The great Danish invasion that opens the book will test that oath as never before.
characters.name: Uhtred

characters.description: King of Wessex, now visibly failing in health but stronger than ever in design: one Christian England, secured for his son Edward. He values Uhtred's sword and mistrusts everything else about him, and as his own death approaches he is chiefly concerned with binding the men who will guard the succession.
characters.name: Alfred

characters.description: Uhtred's Danish wife, sister of Guthred of Northumbria: dark-haired, steady, and the anchor of his household in Lundene. She shares his gods, has borne his children, and is carrying another as the book opens.
characters.name: Gisela

characters.description: A savage Danish earl who leads one of the two great fleets that descend on Wessex, a huge, flamboyant fighter whose banner and temper are equally red. He fights for plunder and glory rather than strategy, goaded on by his woman, the sorceress Skade, and his fury makes him as dangerous to bargain with as to fight.
characters.name: Harald

characters.description: A strikingly beautiful Danish sorceress, Harald Bloodhair's woman, taken captive by Uhtred early in the campaign. Cruel, ambitious, and utterly convinced of her own powers, she is feared for her curses even by hard men. Captivity places her in Uhtred's hands, and she is as dangerous there as anywhere - a woman who ruins the men who hold her.
characters.name: Skade

characters.description: The smiling, endlessly treacherous Danish jarl who escaped the ruin at Beamfleot in the last war. He lands in Kent at the head of his own army, mouthing peace and plotting conquest, using other men's wars - Harald's included - as cover for his own ambitions. No oath, hostage, or baptism binds him for long.
characters.name: Haesten

characters.description: Alfred's daughter and the unhappy wife of Aethelred of Mercia, the woman who was once nearly carried off to a different life by a Norse lover. Braver and cleverer than her husband, she has become a power in Mercia in her own right, loved by its people, and she holds a claim on Uhtred that will outlast every other oath in his life.
characters.name: Aethelflaed

characters.description: Uhtred's Danish foster brother, lord of Dunholm since the fall of Kjartan, married to Brida. Open-handed and warlike as his father was, he keeps a seat at his fire for Uhtred always, and stands for the Danish life Uhtred half-longs to return to: a lord in the north, free of Wessex, its priests, and its oaths.
characters.name: Ragnar

characters.description: The Irish warrior who has been Uhtred's closest friend and second since they were chained together at a slaver's oar: quick, cheerful, deadly, and one of the few constants in Uhtred's shifting fortunes. Where Uhtred fights, Finan is beside him.
characters.name: Finan

characters.description: Alfred's bastard son, once meant for the Church and now one of Uhtred's sworn household warriors. Sober, careful, and quietly capable, he has grown from an unpromising recruit into a man Uhtred relies on, his monkish patience concealing his father's shrewdness.
characters.name: Osferth

recaps.ending: The book ends with Uhtred fighting for Mercia and bound, at last, by an oath he chose. Called back from the Danish north by Aethelflaed's need, he abandons the planned invasion of Wessex he had been plotting with Ragnar and becomes Aethelflaed's sworn man, leading her forces against the Danes ravaging Mercia. Skade, who had cursed Uhtred and gone to Harald Bloodhair, is killed by Harald himself, and the crippled warlord's menace is finally extinguished. The campaign's great stroke is the storming of the Danish camp at Beamfleot, the same creek-side fortress where Uhtred once lost Erik and Sigefrid: the stronghold is taken and burned, its garrison slaughtered or scattered, and Haesten's power is broken, though Haesten himself is elsewhere and survives to scheme again. Gisela is dead, lost in childbirth, and with her much of what tied Uhtred to his old life; his rift with Alfred's court over the cleric he killed in his grief is unhealed, and he did not return to Wessex's service. Instead his oath now rests with Aethelflaed, who has become his lover as well as his lady. Alfred is failing fast, Edward's succession approaches, and Uhtred - the pagan sword on whom the Christian kingdoms depend - ends the book as Mercia's shield rather than Wessex's.
recaps.in_short: Two Danish armies fall on Wessex: the treacherous jarl Haesten lands in Kent talking peace, while the savage Harald Bloodhair burns his way inland. Uhtred captures Skade, Harald's sorceress lover, and crushes Harald's army in battle at Fearnhamme - but Gisela, his wife, dies in childbirth, and when a cleric insults her memory Uhtred kills the man in Alfred's own court. Refusing the humiliating penance and a new oath to young Edward, he flees north with Skade to his foster brother Ragnar at Dunholm, renouncing Wessex and plotting to invade it at the head of a Danish army. Aethelflaed, who holds an old oath of his, calls him back: he abandons the invasion, becomes her sworn man, and leads Mercia's forces against the Danes. Skade, who left him with a curse and returned to Harald, is killed by Harald himself. The campaign climaxes with the storming and burning of the Danish stronghold at Beamfleot, breaking Haesten's power, though Haesten escapes. Uhtred ends the book as Aethelflaed's warrior and lover, bound to Mercia while Alfred fades toward death.

recaps.text: Previously: Uhtred of Bebbanburg - Saxon-born, raised by the Dane Ragnar the Fearless, robbed of his fortress by his uncle - rose to be King Alfred's greatest warrior: he killed Ubba at Cynuit, helped save Wessex at Ethandun (losing his friend Leofric and his lover Iseult), and in the north avenged his foster father, taking Dunholm with his foster brother Ragnar, who killed the murderer Kjartan; Uhtred killed the warlord Ivarr and married Gisela, sister of King Guthred. He survived two years chained at a slaver's oar - gaining his inseparable Irish companion Finan - after Guthred betrayed him. In Sword Song, Alfred's daughter Aethelflaed was married to Uhtred's vain cousin Aethelred of Mercia; Uhtred stormed Lundene and became its governor. Aethelflaed was captured and held at Beamfleot, where she and the Norse lord Erik Thurgilson fell in love; the treacherous jarl Haesten wrecked their planned escape, Erik died at his brother Sigefrid's hand, Uhtred's men destroyed the brothers, and Haesten slipped away. Aethelflaed returned to her loveless marriage carrying a hidden grief and a lasting bond with Uhtred, who serves Alfred's dream of England without sharing it - Bebbanburg still stolen, his oath still binding.

Through the end of Part One (The Warlord): the long-feared storm breaks on Wessex from two directions. Haesten, the smiling and faithless jarl, lands an army in Kent professing peaceful intentions no one believes, while the savage earl Harald Bloodhair brings a second, larger fleet and begins burning his way across the land - the two Danish forces less allies than rivals for the same prize. Early in the campaign Uhtred captures Skade, the beautiful and cruel sorceress who is Harald's woman, and her curses and ambition make her as dangerous a captive as she was an enemy; holding her draws Harald's fury after Uhtred personally. Uhtred, commanding with Finan and his household troops, shapes the defence of Wessex and lures Harald's army into a trap, meeting it in battle at Fearnhamme, where the Danish host is shattered and Harald himself is terribly wounded, his broken remnant driven to bay on an island in the river. The warlord who was to conquer Wessex is crippled and contained - but Haesten's untouched army still watches from the east, waiting to profit from other men's ruin.

Through the end of Part Two (Viking): victory costs Uhtred everything at home. Gisela, his wife of ten years, dies in childbirth, and grief hollows him. When a cleric publicly insults her memory, Uhtred kills the man - a mortal offence in Alfred's Christian court - and the price named is abject penance and a new oath binding him to Alfred's young son Edward. Uhtred refuses. With Skade now his lover and his crews at his back he sails north, renouncing Wessex and its priests, and finds welcome at Dunholm with his foster brother Ragnar and Brida. Through the northern winter he lives as a Dane again and joins in planning the great dream of the northern lords: a Danish invasion to destroy Wessex itself, with Uhtred's knowledge of its defences as the key to the plan. But the old bond holds him yet - word comes from the south that Aethelflaed, Alfred's daughter, unhappy wife of Mercia's lord and the holder of an oath Uhtred cannot shed, needs him. Torn between the Danish life he loves and the woman who trusts him, Uhtred chooses: he abandons the invasion and turns south, a betrayal of Ragnar's hopes that he makes with open eyes.

Through the end of Part Three (Battle's Edge) - the book's close: Uhtred becomes Aethelflaed's sworn man, giving his oath to her rather than to Wessex or its heir, and leads Mercia's forces against the Danes ravaging the land. Skade, who abandoned Uhtred with a curse and made her way back to Harald Bloodhair, meets her end at Harald's own hands, and the crippled warlord's menace is finally extinguished.
