The campaign's great stroke falls at Beamfleot, the creek-side fortress where Uhtred once lost Erik and Sigefrid: he storms the Danish camp, and the stronghold is taken and burned, its garrison slaughtered or scattered and its ships taken or destroyed. Haesten's power is broken - though Haesten himself, elsewhere as ever when the blow lands, escapes to scheme another day. The book ends with Uhtred as Mercia's shield rather than Wessex's: Gisela dead, his rift with Alfred's court unhealed, his oath resting with Aethelflaed, who is now his lover as well as his lady. Alfred is failing fast, Edward's succession draws near, and the pagan warlord on whom the Christian kingdoms depend faces the coming death of a king bound to the one person he chose freely.

characters.description: The commander of the Nightbringers, the army he built out of foresters, refugees and irregulars in the Blood Forest. He is seventeen, married to Tisis Malargos, in possession of an ancient knife that takes a drafter's magic and a set of cards that carry the dead's memories, and he is one of the very few people between the White King's armies and the Chromeria. A significant number of people have decided he is the Lightbringer of prophecy; he has not.
characters.name: Kip

characters.description: Dazen Guile, who took his brother's name and the Prism's office after the False Prism's War and held them for sixteen years. He is blind, has no magic at all, and is out of his father's prison but a long way from the Jaspers, with no title, no proof and nothing left to trade on but the man he actually is.
characters.name: Dazen Guile

characters.description: The White, ruling a Chromeria under siege alongside a father-in-law who holds the emergency office of promachos and does not intend to give it back. She knows now that her husband was Dazen wearing his brother's name, she is fighting a war against her own surviving brother, and the Prism-elect the Chromeria has installed is the son she lost before the war.
characters.name: Karris Guile

characters.description: A Blackguard living as an assassin of the Order of the Broken Eye, invisible when she wants to be, and by now the only person with any chance of finding the Order's hidden master, the Old Man of the Desert. She has spent years doing the Order's work to keep a cover no one can confirm, and the bill for that is coming due.
characters.name: Teia

characters.description: Promachos of the Seven Satrapies: head of House Guile, holder of the wartime office that suspends ordinary government, and the man actually running the defence of the Jaspers. Ancient, brilliant, and entirely willing to spend anyone. Whatever the Chromeria survives, he intends to be what is left standing.
characters.name: Andross Guile

characters.description: Kip's wife and his diplomat, negotiator and political brain, without whom the Nightbringers would have neither supplies nor allies. What began as an arranged marriage for the alliances it bought is now the partnership the whole campaign rests on.
characters.name: Tisis Malargos

characters.description: Koios White Oak, Karris's brother, burned nearly to death in the fire that destroyed their family before the war and now the leader of everything set against the Chromeria. His fleets and armies are converging on the Jaspers, and his banes, the floating islands of luxin in which old gods are seeded, are ripening with them.
characters.name: The White King

characters.description: The Prism-elect: Karris's lost son, a fluent liar and an unhesitating murderer, holding an office that is supposed to be sacred at the exact moment the Chromeria most needs it to mean something.
characters.name: Zymun

characters.description: Aliviana Danavis as she is now: not a drafter but Ferrilux, an old god of superviolet returned into a human body, allied with the White King on terms that are not obviously his. Kip and Karris both knew the girl she used to be.
characters.name: Ferrilux

characters.description: A pirate captain and the finest cannoneer alive, still convinced that his own life is a legend in progress, carrying a blind passenger he cannot decide whether to sell, worship or shoot.
characters.name: Gunner

characters.description: An old sailor working Gunner's ship who happens to bear the name of god, which the crew find funny and which he does not explain. He is unbothered, unhurried, and inclined to answer a question with a better one.
characters.name: Orholam

characters.description: Commander of the Nightbringers under Kip and the conscience of the whole enterprise, still trying to hold an irregular army to the Blackguard's standards in a war that does not reward them.
characters.name: Cruxer

characters.description: The Nightbringers' engineer, a multi-coloured drafter whose spectacles, mechanisms and improvised siege work do as much for the army as its fighters.
characters.name: Ben-hadad

characters.description: A Parian of enormous standing, once commander of the Blackguard, now pulled back toward the country and the throne he spent his career declining. Paria's weight in the coming war depends largely on what he decides to be.
characters.name: Ironfist

characters.description: The Order of the Broken Eye's foremost assassin and Teia's old teacher: a paryl drafter who moves unseen, keeps elaborate private rituals, and takes the teeth of the people he kills. He knows what Teia is and has still not decided what to do about it.
characters.name: Murder Sharp

characters.description: The Guile family's chief slave, who has run Andross Guile's household and his correspondence for decades and knows more of the family's business than any of its members. Elderly, deferential, and permanently in the room.
characters.name: Grinwoody

recaps.ending: The Jaspers hold. The White King's fleet and armies are broken against the islands, with the Chromeria's great mirror array turned on them as a weapon and Kip's Nightbringers arriving in time to matter; Koios White Oak dies, the banes are destroyed, and the gods seeded in them go with them. Zymun's bid for real power ends in his death. Teia kills Murder Sharp and unmasks the Old Man of the Desert, who proves to have been inside House Guile's own household the whole time; the Order is not so much destroyed as taken over. Dazen submits to Orholam's Glare, is judged, and comes out of it with his sight restored, though not his drafting; he survives the battle and is reunited with Karris, who keeps the White's office. Kip learns that the man he called father was his uncle: his father was the real Gavin Guile, which makes Zymun his half-brother and explains a great deal of what Andross has done about him. He and Tisis go back to the Blood Forest to govern it. Andross Guile is alive, still promachos, and still the most dangerous person in the Seven Satrapies. Teia disappears back into the shadows on her own terms. The war is over, the Chromeria has to be rebuilt, and the Guiles are still the Guiles.
recaps.in_short: The White King's armies, fleets and god-bearing banes converge on the Jaspers for the last battle of the war. Kip fights his Nightbringers across the Blood Forest to reach the islands in time; Karris holds the Chromeria beside a father-in-law who will not surrender the promachos's power; Teia hunts the Order of the Broken Eye's hidden master through a city about to be besieged; and Dazen Guile, blind and without magic, comes home by sea in the company of a pirate and an old sailor who bears the name of god. Dazen submits to Orholam's Glare, is judged and forgiven, and gets his sight back if not his drafting. The Chromeria's great mirrors are turned on the enemy fleet, the banes are destroyed, Koios White Oak is killed, and Zymun's ambitions end with him. Teia kills Murder Sharp and finds the Old Man of the Desert inside the Guiles' own household. Kip learns that his father was the real Gavin Guile and the man who raised him was his uncle. Karris remains the White, Andross remains promachos, and Kip and Tisis go home to govern the Blood Forest.

recaps.text: Previously: the man who ruled as Prism for sixteen years was Dazen Guile, wearing the name and face of the brother he beat in the False Prism's War and kept prisoner beneath the Chromeria. Destroying a bane at Ru cost him every colour; he was enslaved, escaped, and was blinded and locked in his own prison by his father Andross, who then had himself made promachos, the wartime office that puts one man over everything. Karris was raised to the White, married and widowed in a matter of weeks, and has since learned who her husband really was. The Prism-elect, Zymun, is the son she bore and lost before the war, and a murderer. The rebellion's leader turned out to be her brother Koios White Oak, believed burned to death years ago and now calling himself the White King; his armies hold Tyrea, Atash and much of the Blood Forest, and his banes, floating islands of luxin, are growing old gods back into the world. Aliviana Danavis took a seed crystal and became one of them, Ferrilux. Kip, driven off the Jaspers, married Tisis Malargos, raised an irregular army in the Blood Forest, broke the siege of Dunbheo and made himself its lord. Teia is still inside the Order of the Broken Eye, hunting its hidden head. And Dazen Guile is out of the cells alive: blind, powerless, and officially dead.

Dazen is at sea, blind and useless, aboard a ship run by the pirate Gunner, who cannot decide what a former Prism is worth. Among the crew is an old sailor who bears the name of god, takes no offence at the jokes about it, and asks Dazen questions he does not want to answer. On the Jaspers, Karris and Andross govern in uneasy tandem while every report says the same thing: the White King is coming to the islands, and he is bringing the banes with him. Kip's Nightbringers hold what they can in the Blood Forest and start the long fight toward the coast. Teia works the Order from inside, closer to the Old Man of the Desert than anyone has ever been and with nobody left to report to.

The war in the north becomes a running campaign: Kip's army is outnumbered everywhere, wins by moving faster than a regular force can, and pays for every win in people he knows by name. Tisis keeps them supplied and allied by negotiation the army mostly never hears about. At the Chromeria, Zymun uses the Prism-elect's office to accumulate real leverage, and Karris has to weigh what she owes a son she never raised against what he is. Andross begins preparing the islands for a siege on a scale nobody living has planned for. Dazen, still at sea, starts to reckon honestly with what he did to win the war and what he did afterwards to keep it.

Teia closes on the Order's structure and finds that it is older, richer and far better placed than the Chromeria ever admitted, with hands inside the institutions that are supposed to oppose it. Murder Sharp knows what she is, or nearly, and the two of them circle each other. On the mainland Kip's reputation runs ahead of him, and with it the argument about the Lightbringer prophecies, which a great many people are now applying to him and which he refuses to claim. The White King consolidates the north and moves his banes toward the Cerulean Sea. Ironfist is pulled back toward Paria and the throne he has spent his life refusing.

Gunner's ship works its way toward the Jaspers, and the old sailor keeps steering Dazen's thinking rather than the vessel. Andross has the Chromeria's great mirror array overhauled: a system built centuries ago to move light around Big Jasper, which can also be aimed. Karris organises the islands for a siege and the evacuation of everyone who cannot fight. Kip's campaign turns from holding ground to racing for the coast, because the Blood Forest cannot be saved if the Jaspers fall. Teia is forced into choices that cost her people she cannot afford to lose.

The banes converge on the Cerulean Sea, and with each one comes a drafter who took a seed crystal and stopped being human: the old gods the Chromeria's whole doctrine says were destroyed. Ferrilux, who used to be Liv Danavis, is one of them, and her alliance with the White King is plainly a matter of convenience on both sides. Paria's decision arrives with Ironfist. Kip reaches the sea with an army that has been fighting continuously for months, and the Chromeria has to decide whether to let a boy nobody appointed bring an unaccountable force onto the islands.

The enemy fleet comes into sight of the Jaspers and the siege begins in earnest: cannon, wights, drafters and the banes themselves grinding at the islands' defences. Karris runs the defence of Big Jasper while Andross runs everything else, and the two of them stop pretending to be allies. Zymun's usefulness runs out and his ambitions turn on the people who installed him. Kip's Nightbringers fight their way into the battle from the outside. Teia, invisible in a city under bombardment, finally has both her old teacher and the Order's master in reach.

Dazen reaches the Jaspers in the middle of the siege, blind, with no rank and nothing but his own account of himself. What is left to him is Orholam's Glare: the mirror array turned on a single person as a judgement, which the tradition says leaves the guilty dead. He goes to it deliberately, is judged for the war, the theft of his brother's name and the sixteen years of prison beneath the tower, and comes out of it alive with his sight restored. His drafting does not come back. The old sailor's identity stops being a joke.

The battle for the islands turns into the kind of fight where the defenders' only advantages are the mirrors and the fact that they have nowhere to retreat to. The great array is aimed at the enemy fleet and used as a weapon. Kip's army takes the fighting to the banes themselves, which have to be destroyed before the gods riding them can be brought fully ashore. Karris fights in the streets of her own city. Teia kills Murder Sharp, which she has been putting off for years, and the Order's chain of command is finally short enough to follow to its end.

Teia follows it and unmasks the Old Man of the Desert. The Order's master has been inside House Guile's own household all along, close enough to Andross Guile to hear everything, for as long as anyone has been looking in the wrong direction. The banes come apart one after another and the gods with them, Ferrilux included, though not without cost to the people who bring them down. Zymun makes his play for something more than the Prism's title and is killed for it. Koios White Oak's army is broken on the Jaspers and Koios dies with it, and the war his fire and his grievance started ends where the Chromeria began.

In the wreckage, the last of the family's secrets is settled. Kip is not Dazen's son. His father was the real Gavin Guile, which makes the man who claimed and raised him his uncle, makes Zymun his half-brother, and accounts for most of what Andross Guile has spent four books doing about him. It changes nothing between Kip and Dazen that either of them wants changed. The Chromeria is standing but hollowed out: a Prism-elect dead, the Blackguard cut to pieces, an entire theology of what luxin is and what the gods were now impossible to keep teaching in the old form.

The war ends with the Jaspers held. Dazen Guile survives with his sight and without his magic, no longer anyone's Prism, and is reunited with Karris, who keeps the White's office and the job of rebuilding the institution under it. Andross Guile comes out of it alive and still promachos, unrepentant and still the most dangerous man in the Seven Satrapies. Teia, having taken the Order's head apart from the inside, does not come back to the Blackguard; she keeps working out of sight, on her own terms. Kip and Tisis go home to the Blood Forest to govern the satrapy his army saved. The gods are gone, the banes are gone, the Chromeria's teaching about what luxin and the old gods were cannot be kept in its old form, and the world has to be put back together by the people who broke it.

characters.description: A United Nations Marine colonel, an Earther career officer with a reputation for competence and for getting difficult assignments finished. He is proud of his service and believes in the institution he serves, and he was the officer ordered to retake a Belt station seized by its own workers. The Belt knows him as the Butcher of Anderson Station; in the present-day frame of the story he is being held to account for it.
characters.name: Fred Johnson

recaps.ending: Fred's account is that the station's occupiers tried to surrender and that the surrender was never allowed to happen: the offer did not reach him in a form he was permitted to accept, his orders were to take the station, and he took it. Everyone aboard died, including people who had put down their weapons and people who had never picked any up. He was decorated for it. When he understood what had actually been refused and by whom, he resigned his commission and said so publicly, which destroyed his career on Earth, embarrassed the United Nations, and made him the one Earther in the system whose word the Belt would provisionally accept. That is what he offers the people holding him: not a defense, but the record. He is not executed. The encounter ends with him alive and no longer belonging to Earth in any meaningful sense, at the start of the long second career that makes him the most effective political operator in the Outer Planets Alliance and the man who runs Tycho Station in the novels that follow.
recaps.in_short: Years after the fact, the man the Belt calls the Butcher of Anderson Station is taken by people who intend to make him answer for it, and the story alternates between that confrontation and the operation itself. Anderson Station was a Belt facility whose workers, pushed past endurance by conditions and by a contract dispute, seized it and killed the people running it. Colonel Fred Johnson of the United Nations Marines was ordered to retake it. The occupiers tried to surrender; the surrender was never permitted to reach him in a form he could accept, and his orders were unambiguous. His marines killed everyone aboard, including those who had already given up. Earth decorated him. When Fred worked out what had been refused and by whom, he resigned publicly and told the truth about it, which ended his career, made him notorious on his own planet, and made him the only Earther the Belt would listen to. Telling that story is what keeps him alive in the present, and what begins his second career in the Outer Planets Alliance.

recaps.text: This novella is a prequel and stands alone. It is set years before the first novel and needs no knowledge of the series beyond its basic setting: humanity has colonized the solar system, Earth's United Nations and the Mars Congressional Republic are the powers that matter, and the people who live and work in the asteroid belt and the outer planets supply both of them while having no government of their own. Belters depend on shipped air, water and contracts controlled from the inner planets, and the political movement that becomes the Outer Planets Alliance is at this point a scattering of angry, unconnected cells. The story concerns a United Nations Marine officer, the name the Belt gave him, and how he came to have it.

The novella runs on two tracks. In the present, Fred Johnson is held by people from the Belt who lost family at Anderson Station and who want the Butcher to account for himself before they decide what to do with him. In the past, Colonel Fred Johnson of the United Nations Marines is ordered to retake that station after its workers, in a dispute over conditions and contracts that escalated past anyone's control, seized it and killed the people in charge. The occupiers attempted to surrender. The offer never reached Fred in a form he was allowed to act on, his orders were to take the station, and his marines killed everyone aboard, including those who had surrendered and those who had never fought. Earth decorated him for it. When he understood what had been refused, and by whom, he resigned his commission and made the reason public, destroying his standing on his own planet. That account is what he gives his captors, and it is what saves him: he leaves the confrontation alive, no longer Earth's man, and takes up the work that makes him the Outer Planets Alliance's most effective figure and the master of Tycho Station.

characters.description: Entering the sixth floor, the Hunting Grounds, where off-world trophy hunters may legally stalk crawlers, Carl upgrades his class to Agent Provocateur and makes good on his pledge to hunt the hunters instead. Armed with the Ring of Divine Suffering, which converts marked kills into raw stats, he opens the floor with a massacre and spends it walking the line between strategist and berserker, all while lawyering the game's own bureaucracy through his new attorney.
characters.name: Carl

characters.description: Carl's talking Persian cat and party leader, saddled this floor with the Legendary Diva class, whose singing-based spells collide with the fact that she cannot sing. Undeterred, she conquers towns by municipal politics, renames one Point Mongo, enters the floor-end gala's talent show and pet contest, and quietly plays a deeper political game with the crawl's alien owners than even Carl realizes.
characters.name: Princess Donut

characters.description: Donut's bound manager, this floor compressed into a tiny, huggable pocket-bear body. His warnings, especially about the addictive Ring of Divine Suffering, and his long memory of the game's history anchor the party as the floor's politics turn lethal.
characters.name: Mordecai

characters.description: Donut's full-grown pet dinosaur and mount, entering a floor that, for once, is home to wild packs of his own kind. As devoted to Donut and as enthusiastically violent as ever.
characters.name: Mongo

characters.description: The party's doppelganger and top-ten crawler, entering the Hunting Grounds intent on shielding Hekla's former Daughters from Eva, a mission she knows will eventually take her out from under Carl's shadow and onto a path of her own.
characters.name: Katia

characters.description: A gentle giant of a crawler, an older Romanian woman who fights alongside her goat Prepotente. Turned into a vampire during the floor's chaos, she becomes the unwilling root of a spreading curse, and the way she chooses to end it becomes one of the book's defining tragedies.
characters.name: Miriam Dom

characters.description: Miriam Dom's companion: a talking goat and one of the crawl's most powerful and strangest competitors, devoted to Miriam with a child's totality. The floor's events push him toward both his greatest feats and his breaking point.
characters.name: Prepotente

characters.description: A mantis huntress of the Hive and one of the most lethal trophy hunters ever to enter the Hunting Grounds, collecting crawler heads as trophies. She marks Carl and Donut as her personal prey, and her contempt for her victims makes her the floor's most intimate enemy.
characters.name: Vrah

characters.description: The tattooed half-naiad Elite from the third floor, returned leading an alliance of were-kin and outcasts. Her father the high elf king is dead, her mother was murdered by naiad dissenters, and her half-sister Imogen now rules the high elves; her war for vengeance, the floor's scripted main story, entwines completely with the crawlers' survival.
characters.name: Signet

characters.description: The doll-headed half-soul of the sand goddess, now the party's screaming, bloodthirsty utility player: missile delivery system, scout, and saboteur. Her hunt for a real body threads through the floor, and being bolted to a hunter's trophy rack barely slows her down.
characters.name: Samantha

characters.description: Queen of the high elves, Signet's half-sister, and host of the Butcher's Masquerade, the gala that closes the floor. Revealed at the party to be a repurposed human, the twin sister of the dead crawler Ifechi, she presides over the celebration under a celestial peace seal that forbids all violence, with a divine boon promised if the night ends without blood.
characters.name: Imogen

recaps.ending: The book ends in the wreckage of the Butcher's Masquerade. Signet sacrificed herself to break the gala's celestial peace seal, giving her tattoos permanent life as she was drawn into the Nothing; in the battle that followed, Mongo and Kiwi killed Vrah, Donut stripped Circe Took's god-armor so her own mantis children destroyed her, the last hunters and high elves were wiped out, and Queen Imogen fell to Prepotente, completing the Vengeance of the Daughter storyline. Donut's potion restored Kiwi to her original ursine form, revealing her as Big Tina's lost mother and completing the Recital quest, and the Sledge's borrowed spell teleported the castle and its NPCs, including the changelings, to safety on the ninth floor. The cost was heavy: Firas, Gwendolyn Duet, Cleiton, and the Popov brothers are dead, though the Popovs, restored to infancy by a rebirth effect, are lifted out of the crawl; Britney is badly burned; Tran lost his legs; and Katia killed Eva at last, unaware Eva's final act was to place the Crown of the Sepsis Whore on her head. Carl and Donut learn their team, the Princess Posse, holds a place in the ninth floor's Faction Wars, secured by Donut's fans and Empress D'Nadia, and Carl closes the floor by telling the watching universe to vote to strip the ninth floor's safety protections. In the epilogue the party skips the seventh floor entirely, Prepotente shattering its level with sponsor-supplied items, and arrives on the eighth, where the crown's curse means only one of Katia or Donut can pass the ninth floor.
recaps.in_short: The sixth floor is the Hunting Grounds, where paying off-world hunters stalk crawlers. Carl opens it with a massacre of hunters in Zockau using the stat-stealing Ring of Divine Suffering, then spends the floor fighting a running war against the mantis huntress Vrah, her mother Circe Took, and the hunter factions, while his lawyer Quasar wrings concessions from Borant, whose ownership shifts to the Valtay mid-book partly through Donut's quiet scheming. Bea, Carl's ex, is revealed alive and paraded on Odette's show. Signet returns leading an army against her half-sister Queen Imogen and the naiad Confederacy; Miriam Dom, turned vampire, chooses death at sunrise to cure the spreading curse, devastating her goat Prepotente; and dinosaur matriarch Kiwi mates with Mongo while the vampiric Big Tina ravages towns. Everything converges at the Butcher's Masquerade, Imogen's peace-sealed gala: Signet sacrifices herself to break the seal, Vrah and Circe and Imogen die in the battle, Kiwi is revealed as Tina's transformed mother, the castle and changelings are teleported to safety, Katia kills Eva but is cursed with the Crown of the Sepsis Whore, and the Princess Posse claims a place in the ninth floor's Faction Wars. The party then skips the seventh floor outright, landing on the eighth.

recaps.text: Previously: Earth became the Borant Corporation's eighteen-floor broadcast dungeon. Carl and the talking cat Princess Donut, with manager Mordecai, dinosaur Mongo, and doppelganger Katia, rose to the top of the crawl across five floors, gathering the sabotage manual called the Dungeon Anarchist's Cookbook, the doll-headed goddess-fragment Samantha, and allies including Louis, Firas, Elle, Imani, and the changeling Juice Box. Carl became an acolyte of the fire god Emberus and assembled the Gate of the Feral Gods, using it to flood Larracos, the ninth floor's great city, after publicly threatening to unleash a feral god there. Maggie My, the Infiltrator who had stolen Chris's body, was finally killed. Enemies remain everywhere: the Skull Empire's royals, the child crawler Lucia Mar, the rampaging Quan Ch, and Eva, the cruelest of Hekla's Daughters, whom Katia intends to thwart by protecting her former teammates. Bea, Carl's ex-girlfriend and Donut's owner, is secretly alive on the surface. The party descends to the sixth floor, the Hunting Grounds, where off-world trophy hunters may enter the dungeon to stalk crawlers, and Carl has pledged to kill every one of them.

The sixth floor opens with lawyers before monsters. The Syndicate liaison Orren relays Borant's demand that Carl surrender the Gate of the Feral Gods, and Carl's new attorney Quasar negotiates its temporary handover in exchange for four mercenaries, including the rock-monsters Bomo and the Sledge, and replicas of two of the gate's spells: a stairwell teleport and the city-moving zerzura. Donut draws the Legendary Diva class, whose song-based spells are useless in the mouth of a cat who cannot sing; Carl upgrades to Agent Provocateur; Mordecai manifests as a tiny pocket bear. Before the hunters are even released, Carl teleports into the town of Zockau, where they gather, and slaughters dozens with bombs and the Ring of Divine Suffering, which converts marked kills into permanent stats, trapping many survivors in the Desperado Club. Wounded in the escape, he is rescued by Miriam Dom, now a vampire, and her goat Prepotente. Mordecai warns him the ring is addictive; the broadcast announces a guild system and, at floor's end, a gala called the Butcher's Masquerade for the top fifty crawlers.

The party digs in for a floor-long war. Katia coordinates knocking down bridges to channel hunter movement while Carl plots a second strike on Zockau, aborted when a note from the mantis huntress Vrah reveals the town is now explosion-proofed and that the Hive has claimed him as prey; the hunters are formally released. Donut solves a hostile town's bureaucracy by killing its mayor and taking the office herself, renaming the place Point Mongo, and the party picks up the Recital quest to investigate dinosaur attacks on the town. Mongo bolts to answer them: he has found a mate, Kiwi, matriarch of an all-female pack of his species. Donut, confronted about her recklessness, admits she is terrified of being left behind, and Carl promises she will always be part of his plans. Signet, the tattooed Elite from the third floor, arrives leading an alliance of were-kin and outcasts: her royal father is dead, her half-sister Imogen rules the high elves, and her mother was murdered by the naiad Confederacy she means to destroy. A looted map shows the hunting factions have carved the floor into territories, with Carl and Donut claimed by the Hive and the Skull Empire.

The floor's politics go galactic. Between Scolopendra lore from Signet's allies and a third sponsorship from the enigmatic Apothecary, Carl and Donut are summoned to Odette's show, where Odette reveals she has been hiding Bea, alive, since the collapse, to keep Borant from repurposing her as a boss. The on-air reunion is a drugged, stage-managed mess, and Donut's parting words to her former owner are not kind. Mid-broadcast, a planet-shaking announcement lands: the Borant Corporation has been split from its government and the Valtay Corporation granted majority ownership, a coup in which Donut, Zev, and Odette all quietly had hands, with Donut admitting she smuggled Valtay agents to the resistance. Back below, the screws tighten: hunters lose outside communication, Carl is booked for a fan convention, Imani becomes guildmaster of the crawlers' new alliance, and Katia formally leaves the party to lead her own team. Elves attack, Samantha is weaponized as a screaming missile, and Carl notches another kill from the hunter faction called the Dream.

Signet's war reaches its first climax at Fort Freedom, the drowned naiad palace. Samantha, promised help recovering her body once the campaign ends, plays decoy at the front door while Signet's forces storm the throne room, and Carl learns the cruelty at the story's root: the dispel-water curse that keeps Signet from her own element was cast by the same high elves who helped the dissenters murder her father the Tsar. The assault ends in a monstrous twist: Claude, a river-beast borough boss who has already devoured the Confederacy and swallows Samantha for good measure, rises from the water, and the allies kill it at the cost of the gentle sage Miss Nadine. The quest updates: Big Tina, the dinosaur ravaging Point Mongo, is named as the Recital quest's culprit, and the Vengeance of the Daughter storyline advances to its final act, kill Queen Imogen at the Butcher's Masquerade, with the high elf castle's loot, possibly including protection from Scolopendra, as the prize. As the party travels on, they walk into the town of Alucarda, whose new mayor is Lucia Mar, just as Carl is teleported away to his convention.

Carl's convention becomes a hostage situation with autographs. Learning his panel will be moderated by Circe Took, mother of both Vrah and a mantis he killed at Zockau, and realizing his guards have drugged away his inhibitions, Carl brawls verbally with her on stage until a robed stranger, one of his own mysterious sponsors, shuts her down. Knowing hunters still leak information from outside, he loudly crowdsources a fake plan to kill Vrah. He returns into an ambush: Lucia Mar camped in the safe room with teleport traps, hunters ringing the exits, and Samantha bolted to Vrah's trophy rack of crawler heads. The real plan unfolds; Carl butchers his way through the cordon and leaves Vrah with a parting gift, an arrow-borne double dose of gonorrhea, before diving into the safe room. The reunion that follows brings lighter news: Katia and Bautista are together, Donut acquires a vocal coach, and the recap broadcast shows Donut fighting Lucia Mar to a draw, killing one of her hell-dogs, while Lucia argues with people who are not there. The floor's strangest thread arrives with Edict, the last male mantis, whose suicide-by-safe-room underlines how thoroughly Vrah's species burns its own.

The middle floor grinds on: Donut collects towns like trophies, a second convention appearance ends with Carl stabbing a show host with a sharpie and earning the threat of a post-crawl warrant, and the Plenty and Apothecary send protection against a spreading new horror, vampirism. Miriam Dom, its unwilling source, calls for help: she is pinned in a ruined town under a paralyzed, fragile Prepotente, while Big Tina, now a vampire herself, raises undead dinosaurs. Fighting through, Carl and Donut learn the dinosaurs were once ursine, transformed in Scolopendra's attack, and that Tina, denied her childhood recital, wants to dance. Miriam's confession is worse: Prepotente's stat-stealing ring accidentally marked her, meaning he cannot heal while she lives, and killing her, the head vampire, will cure every victim. She asks Carl for death; he refuses, and instead sits with her until sunrise does it gently. The cure sweeps the floor, the Creeping Apocalypse world quest begins, and Prepotente, waking to what happened, eats his own ring. Donut charms Kiwi's pack into the party's service as Carl works out that his sponsor the Plenty engineered the whole chain of events.

The endgame board assembles. During the creeper hunt the party meets the high elves and Queen Imogen's familiar: Ferdinand, Bea's other cat, repurposed into a weapon, who nearly kills Donut before her hidden Cockroach ability saves her. The world quest fails, and the punishment reshapes the floor: safe room access now depends on a blood bar filled by killing, and the Gehenna Bramble begins devouring the map, herding every survivor toward the high elf castle. A captured hunter confirms a darker rumor, the dungeon's AI is going primal, ignoring the Syndicate's own court orders, possibly because Borant bought it used and under the table. Signet warns that the dryads may summon the goddess Diwata, and a cryptic sponsor note tells Carl that Circe Took is Diwata's sponsor, with instructions to pass a potion to Donut. A flashback reveals the plan under the plan: Carl and Quasar intend to use the zerzura spell to move an entire city, changelings inside, to the ninth floor. Carl and Donut blackmail their way into the Desperado Club's hunter floor to coordinate with the changelings, and Orren, departing, all but warns them the Masquerade is a trap: Imogen is a country boss built to zero out the top crawlers.

The last days before the gala are spent thinning the herd: guild-wide raids kill hunters by the score, until a church assault triggers Diwata's entry into the realm, and with her a mark of death on Carl for an earlier desecration of her shrine. The goddess ignores the crawlers entirely and beelines for Vrah; Samantha explains Diwata births new forest creatures, and the group realizes she means to cure the mantis's gonorrhea and midwife a new brood. Reaching the next town, Carl briefs Signet honestly: her scripted revenge on Imogen is the floor's climax, designed by showrunners, and he has an alternative plan. Donut has meanwhile amassed a drawer of unexplained gifts from other crawlers' benefactor boxes, a puzzle no one can solve. Carl commits his plan to the cookbook's hidden pages, and the team walks into the Butcher's Masquerade with layered objectives: survive the night, finish the Recital quest, save the changelings, take the castle, and kill Eva, Lucia Mar, and every hunter left alive.

The Masquerade opens under a celestial peace seal: Queen Imogen, revealed to Carl as a repurposed human, the twin sister of the dead crawler Ifechi, will win a divine boon from the god Apito if the night passes without violence, and anyone who breaks the seal will be fed to the Nothing. The guest list is a landmine: Vrah promising Carl a present, Lucia Mar and Eva circling, Empress D'Nadia judging the pet contest, and Signet, invited by Apito personally to test the queen. Carl works the prize counter, buying, among trinkets, the queen's own memorial crystal at Mordecai's urging. Mongo performs in the pet show. Florin pieces together that several personalities share Lucia's head and that her dog is central to it. Outside, baby mantises swarm the castle grounds as Vrah and Circe Took stage their coup; inside, hunters crowd Lucia, goading her to break the seal first. Ferdinand, charmed by Donut, crawls through the ducts into the crawlers' ballroom, and Samantha, doing the same, finds the castle's control room guards already dead. Then Imogen seals every guest inside, and Carl realizes the trap is closing with his own plan half-assembled and his allies outside fighting for their lives.

The seal breaks on Signet's terms. During Donut's talent performance, with Big Tina dancing at last on stage, Signet makes herself the blood sacrifice that animates her own tattoos, breaking the celestial seal as the Nothing takes her, her lost loved ones stepping out of her skin as living beings. In the battle that follows, Mongo and Kiwi kill Vrah; Donut's potion-boosted Laundry Day spell strips Circe Took's god-armor and her own mantis children devour her; the Sledge completes the zerzura, teleporting the castle and its NPCs, changelings included, to the ninth floor; and Donut's mystery potion restores Kiwi to her true ursine form, Big Tina's lost mother, completing the Recital quest. The AI declares a free-for-all boss battle: the last hunters and high elves are annihilated, Gwendolyn Duet and Cleiton die, Tran loses his legs, and Imogen finally falls to Prepotente, completing Vengeance of the Daughter. In the aftermath, Firas and the Popov brothers are dead, the Popovs reborn as infants and lifted out of the crawl; Katia kills Eva at last; and the Princess Posse learns it holds a place in the ninth floor's Faction Wars, secured by Donut's fan club and Empress D'Nadia. Carl uses the live feed to urge the watching universe to vote away the ninth floor's safety protections before the signal cuts.

characters.description: A mathematician and physicist who flew for the Women Airforce Service Pilots during the Second World War and now works as one of the human computers at the national aeronautics agency. A prodigy who went to university years ahead of her age, she is fast and exact with orbital arithmetic and deeply uncomfortable with being looked at; public attention brings on nausea and panic she works hard to hide. She is Jewish, married to the engineer Nathaniel York, and the book opens with the two of them on holiday at a mountain cabin.
characters.name: Elma York

characters.description: Elma's husband, a lead engineer for the national aeronautics agency, calm and quick and entirely unthreatened by his wife being the better mathematician. He treats her calculations as work to be checked rather than opinions to be humored, and his standing inside the program repeatedly gets her arguments a hearing they would not otherwise receive.
characters.name: Nathaniel York

characters.description: Elma's brother, who lives in Charleston, South Carolina with his wife and children. He had polio as a child and gets about with braces and crutches. He and Elma are close, and after the disaster he is the family she has left.
characters.name: Hershel Wexler

characters.description: A decorated military pilot, polished in front of a camera and dismissive of women in cockpits. He and Elma know each other from the war, and whatever passed between them then has left him hostile to her and left her certain he should not be trusted with authority over other people. He is exactly the sort of flier the new space effort will want at the front of it.
characters.name: Stetson Parker

characters.description: The Secretary of Agriculture, and the most senior member of the federal government to survive the destruction of the capital. Sworn in as president in the middle of an unprecedented emergency, he has to decide how much of a wrecked country's remaining capacity to spend on getting off the planet.
characters.name: President Charles Brannan

characters.description: The director of the space coalition's Kansas headquarters, a blunt, cigar-smoking administrator who decides which missions are attempted and which arguments are worth his time. He is not personally opposed to Elma, but he answers to politicians and to public opinion, and he will not spend either on a fight he does not expect to win.
characters.name: Director Clemons

characters.description: A Taiwanese computer and pilot in Elma's department and one of her closest friends. Unflappable at a calculating machine and blunt in private about what the program expects of the women who work for it.
characters.name: Helen Carmouche

characters.description: A computer in Elma's department, part of the group of women whose hand arithmetic stands behind every launch the program attempts.
characters.name: Basira Dutta

characters.description: A pilot and the wife of the governor of Kansas, as comfortable in a ballroom full of politicians as in an aircraft. She reads a room the way Elma reads a slide rule, and her social access to the people who fund the space program turns out to be a form of leverage the program's engineers do not have.
characters.name: Nicole Wargin

characters.description: A former Women Airforce Service Pilot who flew with Elma during the war and now works as a journalist covering the space program. She is warm, sociable and well connected, and she has a professional eye for the story inside a friend's private life.
characters.name: Betty Ralls

characters.description: A computer who comes to work at the program's Kansas headquarters, married to the pilot Eugene Lindholm. She is friendly with Elma and entirely willing to point out that a campaign for women astronauts run by white women is not the same thing as a campaign for all of them.
characters.name: Myrtle Lindholm

characters.description: A Black pilot who flew with the Tuskegee airmen during the war and now works for the space program. Skilled, patient and well aware of the ceiling the corps has set over him, he is one of the fliers pressing for astronaut selection to be opened past the narrow group it currently serves.
characters.name: Eugene Lindholm

characters.description: A Black computer and pilot who joins the group of women building flight hours to prove they meet the astronaut corps' stated requirements, and one of the people who pushes Elma to see whose exclusion her campaign has been quietly overlooking.
characters.name: Ida Peeks

recaps.ending: Elma refuses to be shamed off the flight roster. Rather than let her medication and her treatment be used to disqualify her quietly, she stops hiding them, and the disclosure proves survivable: the program needs the Lady Astronaut more than it needs the pretense that its astronauts are unbreakable. Her standoff with Parker settles into a wary working truce rather than anything like friendship, each of them carrying knowledge about the other from the war. The larger argument is won. The astronaut corps now includes women, the international coalition is committed to a lunar base and an eventual Mars expedition, and the finding that the planet is warming toward uninhabitability is settled policy, even as public patience with the cost of spaceflight begins to fray. The exclusion of Black pilots and computers has been named and pushed at but is nowhere near resolved. Nathaniel remains at the engineering console, their marriage steady and their decision not to have children settled. The book closes with Elma strapped into a capsule on top of a rocket, counting down to her own first flight into space.
recaps.in_short: In an alternate 1952 a meteorite strikes the eastern United States, destroying the capital and killing most of the federal government. Elma York, a mathematician and former wartime pilot, calculates that the water vapor thrown into the atmosphere will drive the climate toward temperatures the planet cannot support, and the surviving government responds by pouring everything into an international space coalition tasked with settling people somewhere other than Earth. Elma and her engineer husband Nathaniel move to its Kansas headquarters, where she works as a computer and watches an astronaut corps be built with no room in it for women. A television appearance makes her famous as the Lady Astronaut, and she spends that fame campaigning for women's selection, widening the argument under pressure from Black colleagues to the people her first version of it left out. Women are admitted and Elma is chosen, over the resistance of the corps' chief, Colonel Stetson Parker. Her severe anxiety and the medication she takes for it are exposed publicly; she survives the disclosure by owning it, and the book ends with her first launch into space.

recaps.text: In an alternate 1952, a meteorite strikes off the eastern coast of the United States, obliterating Washington and killing almost the entire federal government. Elma York, a mathematician and former wartime pilot, is at a mountain cabin with her husband Nathaniel, an engineer for the national aeronautics agency, when the blast wave arrives. They fly out in their small plane through ash and violent turbulence, put down among the injured, and help where they can before a military air base takes them in. News is fragmentary and nobody yet grasps the scale of what has happened. Elma's parents were in the capital and are dead; her brother Hershel, in Charleston, is safe. Working from the little data available, Elma begins calculating how large the impactor was and what it threw into the atmosphere, and the numbers she gets are worse than the ruin already visible.

Elma's arithmetic points past the immediate destruction to something far worse. The impact vaporized an immense quantity of seawater; after a brief cooling period under the dust, that water vapor will trap heat and push the climate toward temperatures the planet cannot support. Getting anyone to act on a woman's calculations takes persistence, Nathaniel's backing and eventually a hearing in front of the new administration. The former Secretary of Agriculture, Charles Brannan, is the senior surviving official and has been sworn in as president, and the government reassembles in Kansas City. The conclusion reshapes national policy: if Earth is going to become uninhabitable, humanity needs somewhere else to live and needs to get there within a lifetime. The space effort is accelerated and made international, the aeronautics agency folded into a coalition whose mandate runs from orbit to the Moon to Mars. Elma and Nathaniel move to Kansas with it, he as a lead engineer and she as one of its computers.

At the coalition's Kansas headquarters Elma works in the computing department alongside Helen Carmouche, Basira Dutta and the other women whose hand calculations underpin every launch, while Nathaniel runs engineering problems upstairs. The program moves fast: test flights, orbital shots, the first men into space. Colonel Stetson Parker, a wartime pilot with a long and bitter history with Elma, is made chief of the astronaut corps and takes the first flight himself. The corps is closed to women by rule and by assumption; Elma, with thousands of flying hours and better mathematics than any of the candidates, is told the qualification is jet test-pilot experience that women are not permitted to obtain. The frustration is sharpened by the program's own logic, since a colony cannot be founded by men alone. Her private difficulty is that any campaign would require her to stand in front of crowds and cameras, which reliably makes her physically ill.

An appearance on a children's television science program turns Elma into a celebrity. Asked what the future holds, she talks about people living on Mars, and the press christens her the Lady Astronaut. She decides to spend the fame: she argues publicly that a colony needs women, organizes the program's women pilots to build and document the flight hours that would make them undeniable, and lobbies anyone who will listen, with Nicole Wargin opening political doors that engineering arguments cannot. Her colleagues Myrtle and Eugene Lindholm and Ida Peeks make it clear that the campaign has been shaped around white women, and Elma, uncomfortable and slow about it, begins widening what she is asking for. Every public appearance costs her: she is sick before broadcasts and shakes through interviews. A doctor prescribes a tranquilizer, and she hides both the prescription and the panic, since anything resembling a psychiatric problem would disqualify her from a flight status she does not yet have.

The campaign works. Under public and political pressure the coalition agrees to select women, and Elma is admitted to astronaut training along with Nicole Wargin, Helen Carmouche, Betty Ralls, Ida Peeks and others, though the class is smaller and more grudging than the argument deserved. Training is physically punishing and socially hostile, with Parker running the corps and making his opinion of the whole exercise plain. Elma stops trying to white-knuckle her anxiety and begins seeing a psychiatrist, which is a greater professional risk than any of the flying, and she keeps it secret from everyone but Nathaniel. Nicole's political instincts and access repeatedly prove more effective than argument. Meanwhile the climate models keep confirming themselves, the coalition commits to a lunar base as the first step toward a Mars colony, and a growing public movement insists the money would be better spent on Earth.

Elma's private life stops being private. Betty, now a working journalist, turns what she knows about her friend into copy, and Elma's anxiety and her medication reach print. The exposure threatens her standing in the corps, hands Parker exactly the lever he has wanted, and forces Elma to choose between denying it, resigning and owning it. Nathaniel's support does not waver, and the two of them are settled in their decision not to have children. Elma also keeps pressing on what her own campaign left out, pushing for the corps and the program to make room for the Black pilots and computers who have been excluded at every stage. The lunar program proceeds, crew assignments begin to matter to people who a year earlier were not permitted to apply, and the opposition to the whole enterprise grows louder as its cost becomes clearer.

Elma refuses to be pushed off the flight roster. Rather than let her treatment be used to disqualify her quietly, she brings it into the open, and the disclosure proves survivable: the program needs the Lady Astronaut more than it needs the pretense that its astronauts are unbreakable. Her long standoff with Parker resolves into a wary truce rather than a friendship, with each of them holding knowledge about the other from the war and neither willing to spend it. The corps now includes women, though the fight to include Black women and men is far from finished, and the coalition is fully committed to a lunar base and an eventual Mars expedition against an accelerating climate deadline. The book ends with Elma in a capsule on top of a rocket, Nathaniel at his console, counting down to her first flight into space.

characters.description: The eldest Baudelaire, a fourteen-year-old inventor who ties back her hair to think. Still a hunted fugitive, she leads her siblings as they hide near Count Olaf himself, hoping to learn the truth about V.F.D. and whether one of their parents survived the fire.
characters.name: Violet Baudelaire

characters.description: The middle Baudelaire, twelve, bespectacled, and endlessly well-read, whose knowledge steers the family. He is desperate to uncover the secret of V.F.D. and to find any answer about his parents' fate.
characters.name: Klaus Baudelaire

characters.description: The youngest Baudelaire, a small child who speaks in short exclamations and bites with four sharp teeth. Increasingly resourceful, she takes on her own disguise as the children hide among performers.
characters.name: Sunny Baudelaire

characters.description: The murderous actor who hunts the Baudelaire fortune, marked by his single eyebrow and ankle tattoo. Traveling with his troupe and his accomplice Esme, he is now searching for a hidden location tied to the secret V.F.D.
characters.name: Count Olaf

characters.description: Count Olaf's fashionable girlfriend and accomplice, cruel and vain, who takes an eager part in his schemes against the children and their fortune.
characters.name: Esme Squalor

characters.description: The fortune-teller of Caligari Carnival, who gazes into a crystal ball and speaks in a heavy, put-on accent, claiming to foresee the future. She has been supplying Count Olaf with information about where to find things he seeks, including the Baudelaires, which makes her a figure the children both fear and hope to learn from.
characters.name: Madame Lulu

characters.description: A performer in the carnival's House of Freaks, a hunchbacked man displayed for the amusement of visitors. Resigned to being treated as an oddity, he works alongside the disguised Baudelaires among the other performers.
characters.name: Hugo

characters.description: A performer in the carnival's House of Freaks, a contortionist who can bend and twist her body into unusual shapes. She is one of the carnival workers the children come to know while hiding among the performers.
characters.name: Colette

characters.description: A performer in the carnival's House of Freaks who is ambidextrous, equally skilled with both hands, and is put on display for it. Ashamed of being treated as a freak for his ability, he works with the other performers alongside the disguised Baudelaires.
characters.name: Kevin

recaps.ending: The Baudelaires learn that clues gathered at the carnival point to a V.F.D. headquarters in the Mortmain Mountains, and that one of their parents may possibly have survived and be connected to it, giving them a new reason to press on. In the climactic chaos of a lion show meant as a grisly spectacle, Madame Lulu is killed by the carnival's hungry lions, and Count Olaf burns Caligari Carnival to the ground, recruiting several of its performers into his troupe. Still disguised and unable to escape, the children are carried onward with the villains toward the mountains. As the group travels, the family is torn apart: Sunny remains in Count Olaf's automobile while Violet and Klaus are riding in a wooden caravan that detaches at the top of a mountain road and goes plunging downhill out of control. The book ends on this separation, with the siblings divided and in danger, and the mystery of V.F.D. and their parents still unresolved.
recaps.in_short: Hidden in the trunk of Count Olaf's car, the Baudelaires arrive at Caligari Carnival, where the fortune-teller Madame Lulu has been secretly feeding Olaf information. To hide and to learn what Lulu knows, the children disguise themselves as carnival performers and join the House of Freaks alongside Hugo, Colette, and Kevin. They discover that Lulu is a fraud playing a dangerous double game, and that clues point to a V.F.D. headquarters in the Mortmain Mountains, possibly linked to a surviving parent. Olaf plots gruesome attractions and decides to destroy the carnival. In the chaos of a deadly lion show, Madame Lulu is killed and Olaf burns the carnival to the ground. Forced to travel onward with the villains toward the mountains, the siblings are split apart: Sunny ends up in Olaf's car while Violet and Klaus ride in a caravan that comes loose at a mountaintop and hurtles downhill, leaving the family separated as the book ends.

recaps.text: The Baudelaire orphans, Violet, Klaus, and Sunny, lost their parents to a fire and have been hunted ever since by the greedy actor Count Olaf, who pursues their fortune through endless disguises and has escaped capture at every turn. Passed through many guardians by the banker Mr. Poe, they befriended the kidnapped Quagmire triplets, chased the meaning of a secret called V.F.D., and were eventually framed by Olaf for the murder of a stranger, Jacques Snicket, becoming fugitives hunted by the law. Hiding at a hospital that then burned down, they escaped by stowing away in the trunk of Olaf's own car, having glimpsed a hint that one of their parents might have survived the fire. Now traveling secretly alongside the very villain who hunts them, the orphans are determined to uncover the truth about V.F.D. and their family, wherever the journey takes them.

The Baudelaires emerge from the trunk of Count Olaf's car at Caligari Carnival, a shabby attraction whose fortune-teller, Madame Lulu, has secretly been supplying Olaf with information, including guidance toward the children themselves. Realizing that Lulu may know the truth about V.F.D. and their parents, the orphans decide to stay close and learn what she knows, but they must hide from Olaf, who frequents her tent. To conceal themselves, the children take on disguises as carnival oddities and join the carnival's House of Freaks, where they meet fellow performers Hugo, a hunchback, Colette, a contortionist, and Kevin, who is ambidextrous. Working among the performers under false identities, the Baudelaires begin trying to draw out what Madame Lulu knows while keeping their true selves hidden from the villain who visits the carnival.

Working in disguise at the carnival, the children try to get Madame Lulu to reveal what she knows about their family and V.F.D., especially any hint that a parent survived the fire. They discover that Lulu is not a true fortune-teller at all but a fraud who uses tricks to fake her predictions, and that she is caught in a dangerous game, giving Count Olaf just enough information to keep him returning while pursuing secret aims of her own. Olaf, meanwhile, grows more menacing, dreaming up cruel new attractions and pressing Lulu to help him locate a hidden place in the Mortmain Mountains. The Baudelaires piece together fragments of the larger secret while staying hidden among the performers, aware that their disguises could fail at any moment and that Olaf's plans are turning ever more deadly.

The children learn that clues point to a hidden V.F.D. headquarters in the Mortmain Mountains, a place that may hold answers about their family and perhaps a surviving parent. Count Olaf resolves to abandon and destroy the carnival and to travel to the mountains himself. Madame Lulu's double game becomes increasingly perilous as Olaf's demands grow, and the villain prepares a horrifying spectacle using the carnival's half-starved lions, meaning to draw a crowd with the promise of violence. Still disguised and now bound up in Olaf's plans, the Baudelaires find themselves swept toward this deadly show, trying to protect themselves and one another while the situation at the carnival spirals toward catastrophe.

In the chaos of the lion show, Madame Lulu is killed by the carnival's hungry lions, and Count Olaf sets fire to Caligari Carnival, burning it to the ground and recruiting several of its performers into his troupe. Unable to escape and still in disguise, the Baudelaires are forced to travel onward with the villains toward the Mortmain Mountains, where they hope to find the truth about V.F.D. and their parents. As the caravan sets out, the family is split apart: Sunny ends up in Count Olaf's automobile, while Violet and Klaus are riding in a wooden caravan that comes loose at the top of a mountain road and goes hurtling downhill out of control. The book ends on this separation, the siblings divided and in danger, with the great mysteries of the series still unsolved and a living parent still only a fragile hope.
